# Bender–Knuth Billiards in Coxeter Groups

**Authors:** Grant Barkley Address: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Email address: gbarkley@math.harvard.edu , Colin Defant Address: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Email address: colindefant@gmail.com , Eliot Hodges Address: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Email address: eliothodges@college.harvard.edu , Noah Kravitz Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08540, USA Email address: nkravitz@princeton.edu and Mitchell Lee Address: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Email address: mitchell@math.harvard.edu

## Abstract

Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system, and write $S=\{s_{i}:i\in I\}$ , where $I$ is a finite index set. Fix a nonempty convex subset $\mathscr{L}$ of $W$ . If $W$ is of type $A$ , then $\mathscr{L}$ is the set of linear extensions of a poset, and there are important Bender–Knuth involutions $\mathrm{BK}_{i}\colon\mathscr{L}\to\mathscr{L}$ indexed by elements of $I$ . For arbitrary $W$ and for each $i\in I$ , we introduce an operator $\tau_{i}\colon W\to W$ (depending on $\mathscr{L}$ ) that we call a noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle; this operator restricts to an involution on $\mathscr{L}$ that coincides with $\mathrm{BK}_{i}$ in type $A$ . Given a Coxeter element $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ , we consider the operator $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}=\tau_{i_{n}}\cdots\tau_{i_{1}}$ . We say $W$ is futuristic if for every nonempty finite convex set $\mathscr{L}$ , every Coxeter element $c$ , and every $u\in W$ , there exists an integer $K\geq 0$ such that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{K}(u)\in\mathscr{L}$ . We prove that finite Coxeter groups, right-angled Coxeter groups, rank-3 Coxeter groups, affine Coxeter groups of types $\widetilde{A}$ and $\widetilde{C}$ , and Coxeter groups whose Coxeter graphs are complete are all futuristic. When $W$ is finite, we actually prove that if $s_{i_{N}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ is a reduced expression for the long element of $W$ , then $\tau_{i_{N}}\cdots\tau_{i_{1}}(W)=\mathscr{L}$ ; this allows us to determine the smallest integer $\mathrm{M}(c)$ such that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{{\mathrm{M}}(c)}(W)=\mathscr{L}$ for all $\mathscr{L}$ . We also exhibit infinitely many non-futuristic Coxeter groups, including all irreducible affine Coxeter groups that are not of type $\widetilde{A}$ , $\widetilde{C}$ , or $\widetilde{G}_{2}$ .

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Linear Extensions and Noninvertible Bender–Knuth Toggles

Let ${P=([n+1],\leq_{P})}$ be a poset whose underlying set is $[n+1]=\{1,\ldots,n+1\}$ . Let $\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ denote the symmetric group whose elements are the permutations of $[n+1]$ (i.e., bijections from $[n+1]$ to itself). We can think of a permutation $w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ as a labeling of $P$ in which the element $i$ receives the label $w(i)$ . We say that the permutation $w$ is a linear extension of $P$ if $i\leq_{P}j$ implies $w(i)\leq w(j)$ . Let $\mathcal{L}(P)$ denote the set of linear extensions of $P$ .

For each $i\in[n]$ , the Bender–Knuth involution $\mathrm{BK}_{i}\colon\mathcal{L}(P)\to\mathcal{L}(P)$ is defined by

$$ \mathrm{BK}_{i}(u)=\begin{cases}u&\mbox{if }u^{-1}(i)\leq_{P}u^{-1}(i+1);\\
(i\,\,i+1)u&\mbox{otherwise,}\end{cases} $$

where we write $(i\,\,j)$ for the transposition that swaps $i$ and $j$ . These involutions are fundamental in algebraic combinatorics [1, 6, 7, 8, 13, 15, 23, 24, 27, 30, 32], largely due to the useful folklore fact that one can reach any linear extension of $P$ from any other linear extension of $P$ via a sequence of Bender–Knuth involutions. Haiman [15] and Malvenuto–Reutenauer [23] found that Schützenberger’s famous promotion and evacuation operators $\mathrm{Pro}$ and $\mathrm{Ev}$ can be written as

$$ \mathrm{Pro}=\mathrm{BK}_{n}\cdots\mathrm{BK}_{1}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{Ev}=(\mathrm{BK}_{1})(\mathrm{BK}_{2}\mathrm{BK}_{1})(\mathrm{BK}_{3}\mathrm{BK}_{2}\mathrm{BK}_{1})\cdots(\mathrm{BK}_{n}\cdots\mathrm{BK}_{2}\mathrm{BK}_{1}). $$

For $i\in[n]$ , define the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle $\tau_{i}\colon\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}\to\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ by

$$ \tau_{i}(u)=\begin{cases}u&\mbox{if }u^{-1}(i)\leq_{P}u^{-1}(i+1);\\
(i\,\,i+1)u&\mbox{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Of course, $\tau_{i}$ is an extension of $\mathrm{BK}_{i}$ from the set of linear extensions of $P$ to the set of all permutations of $[n+1]$ ; it is noninvertible (unless $\mathcal{L}(P)=\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ , i.e., $P$ is an antichain) because $\tau_{i}((i\,\,i+1)u)=\tau_{i}(u)=u$ whenever ${u^{-1}(i)\leq_{P}u^{-1}(i+1)}$ . Defant and Kravitz introduced noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles in [9] in order to define the extended promotion operator $\mathrm{Pro}\colon\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}\to\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ , which is the composition

$$ \mathrm{Pro}=\tau_{n}\cdots\tau_{1}. $$

Hodges further investigated extended promotion in [18]. Restricting extended promotion to $\mathcal{L}(P)$ recovers Schützenberger’s (invertible) promotion operator; hence, we slightly abuse notation by using the same symbol $\mathrm{Pro}$ to denote both of these operators. In a similar vein, we define the extended evacuation operator $\mathrm{Ev}\colon\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}\to\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ by

$$ \mathrm{Ev}=(\tau_{1})(\tau_{2}\tau_{1})(\tau_{3}\tau_{2}\tau_{1})\cdots(\tau_{n}\cdots\tau_{2}\tau_{1}). $$

One of the main results of [9] is that

$$ \mathrm{Pro}^{n}(\mathfrak{S}_{n+1})=\mathcal{L}(P). $$

In other words, if we start with a permutation in $\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ and iteratively apply extended promotion $n$ times, then we will “sort” the permutation to a linear extension (and every element of $\mathcal{L}(P)$ is in the image of $\mathrm{Pro}^{n}$ since $\mathrm{Pro}$ permutes the elements of $\mathcal{L}(P)$ ). In fact, the same argument shows that

$$ \mathrm{Ev}(\mathfrak{S}_{n+1})=\mathcal{L}(P). $$

It is natural to consider other compositions of noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles. For example, gyration [32, 36] is the operator $\mathrm{Gyr}=\mathrm{BK}_{\text{even}}\mathrm{BK}_{\text{odd}}$ , where $\mathrm{BK}_{\text{odd}}$ (respectively, $\mathrm{BK}_{\text{even}}$ ) denotes the product of the Bender–Knuth involutions with odd (respectively, even) indices. By replacing Bender–Knuth involutions with noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles in the definition of gyration, we obtain the extended gyration operator $\mathrm{Gyr}\colon\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}\to\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ . One could ask for an analogue of (2) for extended gyration. As a special case of Corollary 1.24 below, we will find that

$$ \mathrm{Gyr}^{\left\lceil(n+1)/2\right\rceil}(\mathfrak{S}_{n+1})=\mathcal{L}(P) $$

and that the quantity $\left\lceil(n+1)/2\right\rceil$ in this statement cannot be decreased. In fact, one of our results will generalize (2) and (4) to operators obtained by composing $\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{n}$ in an arbitrary order. We will also generalize (3) to any operator obtained by starting with a reduced word for the long element of $\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ and replacing each simple reflection by its corresponding noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle. Moreover, we will state and prove these theorems in the more general setting where the symmetric group $\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ is replaced by any finite Coxeter group. Before stating these results, we need to discuss how to define noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles for general Coxeter groups.

### 1.2. Noninvertible Bender–Knuth Toggles for Coxeter Groups

Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system, and write $S=\{s_{i}:i\in I\}$ , where $I$ is a finite index set. This means that $W$ is a group with a presentation of the form

$$ W=\langle S:(s_{i}s_{i^{\prime}})^{m(i,i^{\prime})}=\mathbbm{1}\text{ for all }i,i^{\prime}\in I\rangle, $$

where $m(i,i)=1$ and $m(i,i^{\prime})=m(i^{\prime},i)\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ for all distinct $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ . The rank of $(W,S)$ is $|S|=|I|$ . We often refer to just the Coxeter group $W$ , tacitly assuming that this refers to the Coxeter system $(W,S)$ .

The Coxeter graph of $W$ is the undirected edge-labeled graph $\Gamma_{W}$ with vertex set $I$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $i^{\prime}$ are joined by an edge labeled $m(i,i^{\prime})$ whenever $m(i,i^{\prime})\geq 3$ . It is typical to omit the label “ $3$ ” in drawings of Coxeter graphs. For $J\subseteq I$ , the corresponding (standard) parabolic subgroup is the subgroup $W_{J}$ of $W$ generated by $\{s_{i}:i\in J\}$ . The pair $(W_{J},\{s_{i}:i\in J\})$ is a Coxeter system, and $\Gamma_{W_{J}}$ is the subgraph of $\Gamma_{W}$ induced by $J$ .

The root space of $W$ is the vector space $V=\mathbb{R}^{I}$ . Let $\{\alpha_{i}:i\in I\}$ be the standard basis of $V$ ; we call the elements of this basis the simple roots. For each pair $\{i,i^{\prime}\}$ of indices in $I$ such that $m(i,i^{\prime})=\infty$ , choose a real number $\mu_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}\geq 1$ . Define a symmetric bilinear form $B\colon V\times V\to\mathbb{R}$ by setting

$$ B(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i^{\prime}})=\begin{cases}-\cos(\pi/m(i,i^{\prime}))&\mbox{if $m(i,i^{\prime})<\infty$;}\\
-\mu_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}&\mbox{if $m(i,i^{\prime})=\infty$}\end{cases} $$

for all $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ and extending bilinearly; we say $B$ is induced by $W$ .11 1 With this definition, $B$ is not uniquely determined by $W$ since we can freely choose the number $\mu_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}\geq 1$ whenever $m(i,i^{\prime})=\infty$ . However, all of our results and arguments outside of Section 3.5 are independent of these choices. Thus, unless explicitly stated otherwise, we will assume $\mu_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}=1$ whenever $m(i,i^{\prime})=\infty$ so that we may refer to $B$ as “the” bilinear form induced by $W$ . The standard geometric representation of $W$ is the faithful representation $\rho\colon W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ defined by $\rho(s_{i})\beta=\beta-2B(\beta,\alpha_{i})\alpha_{i}$ . We often write $w\beta$ to mean $\rho(w)\beta$ . The set $\Phi=\{w\alpha_{i}:w\in W,\,\,i\in I\}$ is called the root system of $W$ ; its elements are called roots. We say $\beta\in\Phi$ is positive if it is a nonnegative linear combination of the simple roots. We say $\beta$ is negative if $-\beta$ is positive. Let $\Phi^{+}$ and $\Phi^{-}$ denote the set of positive roots and the set of negative roots, respectively. We have $\Phi^{-}=-\Phi^{+}$ and $\Phi=\Phi^{+}\sqcup\Phi^{-}$ . We say that a subset $R\subseteq\Phi$ is closed if whenever $\beta,\beta^{\prime}\in R$ and $a,a^{\prime}\geq 0$ satisfy $a\beta+a^{\prime}\beta^{\prime}\in\Phi$ , we have $a\beta+a^{\prime}\beta^{\prime}\in R$ . We say that $R\subseteq\Phi$ is antisymmetric if $R\cap(-R)=\varnothing$ .

Let $V^{*}$ be the dual space of $V$ . For $\beta\in\Phi$ , consider the hyperplane

$$ \mathrm{H}_{\beta}=\{f\in V^{*}:f(\beta)=0\} $$

in $V^{*}$ . The Coxeter arrangement of $W$ is the collection $\mathcal{H}_{W}=\{\mathrm{H}_{\beta}:\beta\in\Phi\}$ . A region of $\mathcal{H}_{W}$ is the closure of a connected component of $V^{*}\setminus\bigcup_{\beta\in\Phi}\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ . Consider the region

$$ {\mathbb{B}}=\{f\in V^{*}:f(\alpha_{i})\geq 0\text{ for all }i\in I\}; $$

the set of bounding walls of ${\mathbb{B}}$ is $\{\mathrm{H}_{\alpha_{i}}:i\in I\}$ . There is a right action of $W$ on $V^{*}$ determined by the condition that $(fw)(\beta)=f(w\beta)$ for all $w\in W$ , $\beta\in V$ , and $f\in V^{*}$ ; this induces an action of $W$ on the set of regions of $\mathcal{H}_{W}$ . The set ${\mathbb{B}}W\subseteq V^{*}$ is called the Tits cone. The elements of $W$ are in bijection with the regions of $\mathcal{H}_{W}$ that are contained in the Tits cone via the bijection $u\mapsto\mathbb{B}u$ . The positive projectivization of the Tits cone is the quotient

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B}W)=(\mathbb{B}W\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{R}_{>0}. $$

We may view each $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ as a hyperplane in $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B}W)$ and view $\mathcal{H}_{W}$ as a hyperplane arrangement in $\mathbb{P}({\mathbb{B}W})$ . Two distinct hyperplanes $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ and $\mathrm{H}_{\beta^{\prime}}$ intersect in $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B}W)$ if and only if $|B(\beta,\beta^{\prime})|<1$ . It is possible to equip $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B}W)$ with a (not necessarily Riemannian) metric such that for all distinct $\beta,\beta^{\prime}\in\Phi$ with $|B(\beta,\beta^{\prime})|<1$ , the hyperplanes $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ and $\mathrm{H}_{\beta^{\prime}}$ intersect at an angle $\theta$ that satisfies $\lvert\cos(\theta)\rvert=\lvert B(\beta,\beta^{\prime})\rvert$ .

For $\beta\in\Phi$ , define the corresponding half-spaces

$$ H_{\beta}^{+}=\{w\in W:w\beta\in\Phi^{+}\}\quad\text{and}\quad H_{\beta}^{-}=\{w\in W:w\beta\in\Phi^{-}\}. $$

Observe that these two sets are complements of one another in $W$ and that $H_{\beta}^{-}=H_{-\beta}^{+}$ . Note that $\mathbb{B}H_{\beta}^{+}$ is the part of the Tits cone that lies on one side of $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ , while $\mathbb{B}H_{\beta}^{-}$ is the part of the Tits cone that lies on the other side.

For nonempty $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ , define

$$ \mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})=\{\beta\in\Phi:\mathscr{L}\subseteq H_{\beta}^{+}\}. $$

Note that $\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ is closed and antisymmetric. The convex hull of $\mathscr{L}$ is the intersection

$$ \bigcap_{\beta\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})}H_{\beta}^{+} $$

of all of the half-spaces that contain $\mathscr{L}$ (if $\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})=\varnothing$ , this intersection is interpreted as all of $W$ ). We say $\mathscr{L}$ is convex if it is equal to its own convex hull. In other words, a set is convex if it is an intersection of half-spaces.

#### Remark 1.1.

Let $\mathrm{Cay}(W,S)$ be the left Cayley graph of $W$ generated by $S$ . It is known (see [35, Theorem 2.19]) that a set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ is convex if and only if every minimum-length path in $\mathrm{Cay}(W,S)$ between two elements of $\mathscr{L}$ has all of its vertices in $\mathscr{L}$ . This implies that the convex hull of a finite set is finite.

#### Definition 1.2.

Fix a nonempty convex subset $\mathscr{L}$ of $W$ . For each $i\in I$ , define the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle $\tau_{i}\colon W\to W$ by

$$ \tau_{i}(u)=\begin{cases}u&\mbox{if $u^{-1}\alpha_{i}\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$;}\\
s_{i}u&\mbox{if $u^{-1}\alpha_{i}\not\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$.}\end{cases} $$

The preceding definition does not rely on the geometry of the Coxeter arrangement, but it has the following geometric interpretation. If we identify each element $w\in W$ with the region ${\mathbb{B}w}$ of the Coxeter arrangement, then $\mathrm{H}_{u^{-1}\alpha_{i}}$ is the unique hyperplane separating $u$ from $s_{i}u$ . The toggle $\tau_{i}$ is defined so that $\tau_{i}(u)=u$ if and only if $\mathscr{L}\cup\{u\}$ lies entirely on one side of $\mathrm{H}_{u^{-1}\alpha_{i}}$ . Equivalently, $\tau_{i}(u)=s_{i}u$ if and only if there is an element of $\mathscr{L}$ on the same side of $\mathrm{H}_{u^{-1}\alpha_{i}}$ as $s_{i}u$ . Thus, moving from $u$ to $\tau_{i}(u)$ cannot take us “strictly away from” the convex set $\mathscr{L}$ .22 2 One can also define the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles using the set of reflections rather than the root system (using (10) below). Although this perspective would make many of our proofs more complicated, it will be somewhat helpful in Section 10.

#### Example 1.3.

Let $W=\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ , and let $S=\{s_{i}:i\in[n]\}$ , where $s_{i}=(i\,\,i+1)$ . Then $(\mathfrak{S}_{n+1},S)$ is the Coxeter system of type $A_{n}$ . We can identify $V$ with the vector space

$$ \{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n+1})\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n+1}=0\} $$

via the isomorphism that sends the simple root $\alpha_{i}$ to $e_{i}-e_{i+1}$ , where $e_{j}$ denotes the $j$ -th standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ . We have

$$ \Phi^{+}=\{e_{i}-e_{j}:1\leq i<j\leq n+1\}\quad\text{and}\quad\Phi^{-}=\{e_{j}-e_{i}:1\leq i<j\leq n+1\}. $$

The action of $W$ on $\Phi$ is given by $w(e_{i}-e_{j})=e_{w(i)}-e_{w(j)}$ . Hence, for any root $e_{i}-e_{j}\in\Phi$ , we have

$$ H_{e_{i}-e_{j}}^{+}=\{w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}:w(i)<w(j)\}. $$

Let $\mathscr{L}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ be a nonempty set. We may define a relation $\leq_{\mathscr{L}}$ on $[n+1]$ by declaring that $i\leq_{\mathscr{L}}j$ if and only if either $i=j$ or $e_{i}-e_{j}\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ . Since $\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ is closed and antisymmetric, the relation $\leq_{\mathscr{L}}$ is a partial order. By the above discussion, the convex hull of $\mathscr{L}$ is precisely the set of linear extensions of $([n+1],\leq_{\mathscr{L}})$ . In this way, nonempty convex subsets of $\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ correspond bijectively to partial orders on $[n+1]$ , and the root-theoretic definition of $\tau_{i}$ in Definition 1.2 agrees with the poset-theoretic definition in (1).

### 1.3. Bender–Knuth Billiards

Fix a nonempty convex subset $\mathscr{L}$ of a Coxeter group $W$ , and use this convex set to define the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles $\tau_{i}$ for $i\in I$ , as in Definition 1.2.

Let $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ be an ordering of the elements of $I$ . It is convenient to take $i_{k+n}=i_{k}$ for every positive integer $k$ , thereby obtaining an infinite periodic sequence $i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},\ldots$ . If we start with an element $u_{0}\in W$ and apply the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles in the order $\tau_{i_{1}},\tau_{i_{2}},\tau_{i_{3}},\ldots$ , we obtain a sequence $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ , where $u_{j}=\tau_{i_{j}}(u_{j-1})$ for each $j\geq 1$ . We call this sequence a (Bender–Knuth) billiards trajectory. We can draw the billiards trajectory in $\mathbb{P}({\mathbb{B}W})$ . In each of Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4, we have drawn a billiards trajectory using a sequence of arrows, where each arrow points from $\mathbb{B}u_{j-1}$ to $\mathbb{B}u_{j}$ for some $j$ .

We say a hyperplane $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ is a one-way mirror if $\beta\in(\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})\cup(-\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L}))$ ; otherwise, we say that $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ is a window. Somewhat informally, we imagine the billiards trajectory is the trajectory of a beam of light that starts at $u_{0}$ . Each window allows the light to pass through it in either direction. By contrast, if $\beta\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ , then $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ is a one-way mirror that allows the light to pass from $H_{\beta}^{-}$ to $H_{\beta}^{+}$ but reflects light that tries to pass in the other direction.

#### Remark 1.5.

In each of Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4, we have drawn a thin, cyan, piecewise linear path that reflects off of the one-way mirrors according to the usual billiards rule (i.e., that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection), which has been studied vigorously and fruitfully in dynamics [16, 20, 25, 34]. We call this cyan path a light beam. Our Bender–Knuth billiards trajectory appears to follow alongside the light beam, so it can be seen as a discretization of the light beam. It is natural to ask under what conditions a Bender–Knuth billiards trajectory will discretize a light beam (and how to even rigorously formalize this idea). We will discuss this in Section 11, where we will see that the Bender–Knuth billiards trajectory discretizes a light beam whenever $|I|\leq 3$ or the Coxeter element $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ is bipartite.

Given a word $\mathsf{w}=i_{M}\cdots i_{1}$ over the alphabet $I$ , it will be convenient to define the composition of toggles

$$ \tau_{\mathsf{w}}=\tau_{i_{M}}\cdots\tau_{i_{1}}. $$

A (standard) Coxeter element of $W$ is an element obtained by multiplying the elements of $S$ together in some order so that each simple reflection appears exactly once in the product. Such an ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ of $I$ gives rise to a reduced word $\mathsf{c}=i_{n}\cdots i_{1}$ representing a Coxeter element $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ . Let

$$ \mathrm{Pro}_{c}=\tau_{\mathsf{c}}=\tau_{i_{n}}\cdots\tau_{i_{1}}. $$

Because $\tau_{i}\tau_{i^{\prime}}=\tau_{i^{\prime}}\tau_{i}$ whenever $m(i,i^{\prime})=2$ , it follows from Matsumoto’s theorem (Theorem 2.1 below) that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}$ depends only on $c$ and not on the particular reduced word $\mathsf{c}$ . Each operator $\tau_{i}$ restricts to a bijection from $\mathscr{L}$ to itself; thus, $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}$ also restricts to a bijection from $\mathscr{L}$ to itself. An element $u\in W$ is called a periodic point of $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}$ if there exists an integer $K\geq 1$ such that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{K}(u)=u$ .

Because noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles never cause the billiards trajectory to move “strictly away from” $\mathscr{L}$ , one might expect (as we did for a while) that every periodic billiards trajectory must lie in $\mathscr{L}$ . As we will see, this is not always the case. Let us establish some terminology to describe the various scenarios that can occur.

#### Definition 1.6.

Let $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ be a nonempty convex set, and define the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles with respect to $\mathscr{L}$ . Let $c$ be a Coxeter element of $W$ .

- • We say $\mathscr{L}$ is heavy with respect to $c$ if every periodic point of $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}$ lies in $\mathscr{L}$ .

- • We say $\mathscr{L}$ is superheavy with respect to $c$ if for every $u\in W$ , there exists a nonnegative integer $K$ such that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{K}(u)\in\mathscr{L}$ .33 3 We imagine that $\mathscr{L}$ is a black hole that always pulls light into it. It would be more consistent with astrophysical terminology to use the words “massive” and “supermassive” rather than “heavy” and “superheavy”. However, doing so would prevent us from writing Footnote 4.

Note that if $\mathscr{L}$ is superheavy with respect to $c$ , then it is heavy with respect to $c$ . The two definitions are equivalent if $W$ is finite.

#### Remark 1.7.

One could rephrase Definition 1.6 in the language of billiards trajectories instead of the operators $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}$ . A convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ is heavy with respect to a Coxeter element $s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ if and only if every periodic billiards trajectory (defined with respect to the convex set $\mathscr{L}$ and the ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ of $I$ ) lies in $\mathscr{L}$ . Similarly, $\mathscr{L}$ is superheavy with respect to $s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ if and only if every billiards trajectory eventually reaches $\mathscr{L}$ .

As an illustration of the preceding definitions, Theorem 1.15 (below) will tell us that every nonempty convex subset of $\widetilde{A}_{2}$ is heavy with respect to the Coxeter element $s_{2}s_{1}s_{0}$ . This means that for every nonempty convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq\widetilde{A}_{2}$ and every starting element $u_{0}\in W\setminus\mathscr{L}$ , the billiards trajectory

$$ u_{0},\tau_{0}(u_{0}),\tau_{1}\tau_{0}(u_{0}),\tau_{2}\tau_{1}\tau_{0}(u_{0}),\tau_{0}\tau_{2}\tau_{1}\tau_{0}(u_{0}),\ldots $$

is not periodic. This does not necessarily imply that the billiards trajectory eventually reaches the set $\mathscr{L}$ . For example, Figure 3 depicts a billiards trajectory in $\widetilde{A}_{2}$ that does not reach $\mathscr{L}$ . Hence, the convex set depicted in Figure 3 is heavy but not superheavy with respect to $s_{2}s_{1}s_{0}$ .

#### Proposition 1.8.

Let $W$ be a Coxeter group, and let $c$ be a Coxeter element of $W$ . The following are equivalent.

- (i) Every nonempty convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ is heavy with respect to $c$ .

- (ii) Every nonempty finite convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ is heavy with respect to $c$ .

- (iii) Every nonempty finite convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ is superheavy with respect to $c$ .

Note that by the paragraph preceding Proposition 1.8, the condition that every nonempty convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ is superheavy with respect to $c$ is strictly stronger than the conditions (i), (ii), and (iii) of Proposition 1.8.

The preceding proposition naturally motivates the following definitions, which are central to the present work.

#### Definition 1.9.

- • We say a Coxeter element $c\in W$ is futuristic if every nonempty convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ is heavy with respect to $c$ (i.e., $c$ satisfies the three equivalent conditions of Proposition 1.8).

- • We say a Coxeter element $c\in W$ is superfuturistic if every nonempty convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ is superheavy with respect to $c$ .

- • We say the Coxeter group $W$ is futuristic if every Coxeter element of $W$ is futuristic (equivalently, if every nonempty convex subset of $W$ is heavy with respect to every Coxeter element of $W$ ).44 4 In the movie Back to the Future, Doc asks Marty, “Why are things so heavy in the future?”

- • We say the Coxeter group $W$ is superfuturistic if every Coxeter element of $W$ is superfuturistic (equivalently, if every nonempty convex subset of $W$ is superheavy with respect to every Coxeter element of $W$ ).

- • We say the Coxeter group $W$ is ancient if no Coxeter element of $W$ is futuristic.

### 1.4. Main Results

Our overarching goal is to understand which Coxeter groups are futuristic and which are ancient. We begin with the following propositions, which state that the class of futuristic Coxeter groups and the class of non-ancient Coxeter groups are in some sense hereditary.

#### Proposition 1.12.

Let $W_{J}$ be a standard parabolic subgroup of a Coxeter group $W$ .

- (i) If $W$ is futuristic, then $W_{J}$ is futuristic.

- (ii) If $W_{J}$ is ancient, then $W$ is ancient.

Let us say a Coxeter group is minimally non-futuristic if it is not futuristic and all of its proper standard parabolic subgroups are futuristic. Likewise, say a Coxeter group is minimally ancient if it is ancient and none of its proper standard parabolic subgroups are ancient. Proposition 1.12 reduces the problem of characterizing futuristic Coxeter groups and ancient Coxeter groups to the problem of characterizing minimally non-futuristic Coxeter groups and minimally ancient Coxeter groups.

Another tool that we can use to determine whether or not a Coxeter group is futuristic comes from the technique of folding, defined in Section 3.5.

#### Proposition 1.13.

Let $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ be a folding of a Coxeter group $W$ . If $W$ is futuristic, then $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ is futuristic.

### 1.5. Finite Coxeter Groups

Let us now assume that $W$ is a finite Coxeter group. Theorem 1.14 tells us that $W$ is superfuturistic; this implies that for every Coxeter element $c$ of $W$ , there exists a nonnegative integer $K$ satisfying $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{K}(W)=\mathscr{L}$ for every nonempty convex subset $\mathscr{L}$ of $W$ . Our proof of Theorem 1.14 will actually determine the smallest such integer $K$ (in terms of $c$ ).

Because $W$ is finite, it has a unique element of maximum length; this element is called the long element and is denoted by $w_{\circ}$ . The following result generalizes (3) and is new even in type $A$ .

#### Theorem 1.22.

If $W$ is finite and $i_{N}\cdots i_{1}$ is a reduced word for $w_{\circ}$ , then

$$ \tau_{i_{N}}\cdots\tau_{i_{1}}(W)=\mathscr{L}. $$

Theorem 1.22 is tight in the sense that there exists a choice of $\mathscr{L}$ such that

$$ \tau_{i_{N-1}}\cdots\tau_{i_{1}}(W)\neq\mathscr{L}. $$

For example, this is the case if $\mathscr{L}=\{w_{\circ}\}$ , because then $\tau_{i_{N-1}}\cdots\tau_{i_{1}}(\mathbbm{1})=s_{i_{N-1}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}\neq w_{\circ}$ (in fact, the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles generate the 0-Hecke monoid of $W$ [17, 19] in this particular case).

#### Remark 1.23.

If $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ satisfy $m(i,i^{\prime})=2$ , then $\tau_{i}$ and $\tau_{i^{\prime}}$ commute. What makes Theorem 1.22 nontrivial is the fact that the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles do not (in general) satisfy the other braid relations of $W$ . For example, when $W=\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ and $i\in[n]$ , the operators $\tau_{i}\tau_{i+1}\tau_{i}$ and $\tau_{i+1}\tau_{i}\tau_{i+1}$ are generally not equal.

Let $\mathsf{c}$ be a reduced word for a Coxeter element $c$ of $W$ . For $j\geq 1$ , let $\mathsf{c}^{j}$ denote the concatenation of $j$ copies of $\mathsf{c}$ . Let $\mathrm{M}(c)$ be the smallest positive integer $k$ such that $\mathsf{c}^{k}$ contains a reduced word for $w_{\circ}$ as a subword. (The number $\mathrm{M}(c)$ depends only on $c$ , not on the particular reduced word $\mathsf{c}$ .) In Section 4, we will describe how to compute $\mathrm{M}(c)$ explicitly using diagrams called combinatorial AR quivers. The next result, which we obtain as a corollary of Theorem 1.22, generalizes (2); as discussed in Example 1.25, it also implies the new result (4).

#### Corollary 1.24.

If $c$ is a Coxeter element of a finite Coxeter group $W$ , then

$$ \mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{\mathrm{M}(c)}(W)=\mathscr{L}. $$

Corollary 1.24 is tight in the sense that there exists a choice of $\mathscr{L}$ such that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{\mathrm{M}(c)-1}(W)\neq\mathscr{L}$ . For example, this is the case if $\mathscr{L}=\{w_{\circ}\}$ .

#### Example 1.25.

If $W$ is a (not necessarily finite) Coxeter group whose Coxeter graph is bipartite, then we can consider a bipartition $I=Q\sqcup Q^{\prime}$ and write $c_{Q}=\prod_{i\in Q}s_{i}$ and $c_{Q^{\prime}}=\prod_{i\in Q^{\prime}}s_{i}$ . Then $c_{Q^{\prime}}c_{Q}$ is called a bipartite Coxeter element of $W$ .

Now, assume $W$ is finite and irreducible. The Coxeter number of $W$ is the quantity $h=|\Phi|/|S|$ . It is known that $\Gamma_{W}$ must be bipartite, so it has a bipartite Coxeter element $c=c_{Q^{\prime}}c_{Q}$ . It is known [3, $\lx@sectionsign$ V.6 Exercise 2] that $\mathrm{M}(c_{Q^{\prime}}c_{Q})=\left\lceil h/2\right\rceil$ , so Corollary 1.24 tells us that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c_{Q^{\prime}}c_{Q}}^{\left\lceil h/2\right\rceil}(W)=\mathscr{L}$ .

When $W=\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ and $S=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\}$ , where $s_{i}=(i\,\,i+1)$ , the Coxeter graph $\Gamma_{W}$ is a path in which $i$ is adjacent to $i+1$ for each $i\in[n-1]$ . In this case, we can take $Q$ (respectively, $Q^{\prime}$ ) to be the set of odd-indexed (respectively, even-indexed) simple reflections. Then $\mathrm{Pro}_{c_{Q^{\prime}}c_{Q}}=\mathrm{Gyr}$ . The Coxeter number of $\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ is $n+1$ , so we obtain the identity (4).

The proofs of (2) and (3) from [9] are quite specific to the extended promotion and extended evacuation operators (they rely on the notion of a promotion chain), and they do not generalize to other operators such as extended gyration. ## 2. Preliminaries

This section discusses relevant background information about Coxeter groups, largely drawing from the standard reference [2]. We assume that the reader is familiar with the classifications of finite Coxeter groups and affine Coxeter groups and the standard notation used to refer to such groups ([2, Appendix A1]).

Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system whose set of simple reflections $S=\{s_{i}:i\in I\}$ is indexed by a finite set $I$ . A word is a sequence $\mathsf{w}=i_{M}\cdots i_{1}$ of elements of $I$ ; the integer $M$ is called the length of $\mathsf{w}$ . We say the word $\mathsf{w}=i_{M}\cdots i_{1}$ represents the product $w=s_{i_{M}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ of the corresponding simple reflections. A reduced word for an element $w\in W$ is a word that represents $w$ and has minimum possible length. If $i_{M}\cdots i_{1}$ is a reduced word for $w$ , then we call the expression $s_{i_{M}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ a reduced expression for $w$ . The length of $w$ , denoted $\ell(w)$ , is defined to be the length of a reduced word for $w$ . A reflection is an element of $W$ that is conjugate to a simple reflection. We write $T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\,\,s\in S\}$ for the set of reflections of $W$ . For $w\in W$ , the set of right inversions of $w$ is $\mathrm{Inv}(w)=\{t\in T:\ell(wt)<\ell(w)\}$ . We have $\left\lvert\mathrm{Inv}(w)\right\rvert=\ell(w)$ .

Given a word $\mathsf{w}=i_{M}\cdots i_{1}$ , we write $\tau_{\mathsf{w}}=\tau_{i_{M}}\cdots\tau_{i_{1}}$ . One can apply a commutation move to $\mathsf{w}$ by swapping two consecutive letters $i$ and $i^{\prime}$ that satisfy $m(i,i^{\prime})=2$ . We say that two words $\mathsf{x}$ and $\mathsf{y}$ are commutation equivalent, denoted $\mathsf{x}\equiv\mathsf{y}$ , if $\mathsf{y}$ can be obtained from $\mathsf{x}$ via a sequence of commutation moves. Note that two commutation equivalent words represent the same element of $W$ . Moreover, if $\mathsf{x}\equiv\mathsf{y}$ , then $\tau_{\mathsf{x}}=\tau_{\mathsf{y}}$ .

Given symbols $\xi$ and $\xi^{\prime}$ and a positive integer $d$ , let us write

$$ [\xi\mid\xi^{\prime}]_{d}=\underbrace{\cdots\xi^{\prime}\xi\xi^{\prime}}_{d} $$

for the string of length $d$ that alternates between $\xi$ and $\xi^{\prime}$ and ends with $\xi^{\prime}$ . For example, we have ${[\xi\mid\xi^{\prime}]_{4}=\xi\xi^{\prime}\xi\xi^{\prime}}$ and ${[\xi\mid\xi^{\prime}]_{5}=\xi^{\prime}\xi\xi^{\prime}\xi\xi^{\prime}}$ .

For $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ , it follows from the defining presentation of $W$ in (5) that the words

$$ [i\mid i^{\prime}]_{m(i,i^{\prime})}\quad\text{and}\quad[i^{\prime}\mid i]_{m(i,i^{\prime})} $$

represent the same element of $W$ . If $\mathsf{w}$ is a word that contains one of the two alternating words in (8) as a consecutive factor, then we can perform a braid move on $\mathsf{w}$ by replacing that consecutive factor with the other alternating word in (8) (if $m(i,i^{\prime})=2$ , then this braid move is a commutation move). If $\mathsf{w}$ contains two consecutive occurrences of the same letter, then we can perform a nil move on $\mathsf{w}$ by deleting those two consecutive letters. If a word $\mathsf{w}$ can be obtained from a word $\mathsf{v}$ via a sequence of braid moves and nil moves, then $\mathsf{v}$ and $\mathsf{w}$ represent the same element of $W$ .

#### Theorem 2.1 (Matsumoto’s Theorem [2, Theorem 3.3.1]).

Let $\mathsf{v}$ and $\mathsf{w}$ be words that represent the same element of $W$ . If $\mathsf{w}$ is reduced, then $\mathsf{w}$ can be obtained from $\mathsf{v}$ via a sequence of braid moves and nil moves.

As in Section 1.2, let $V$ denote the root space of $W$ . For $i\in I$ , let $\alpha_{i}$ denote the simple root indexed by $i$ . Then $V$ is a $W$ -module under the standard geometric representation, and there is a $W$ -invariant symmetric bilinear form $B\colon V\times V\to\mathbb{R}$ induced by $W$ . Let $\Phi=\{w\alpha_{i}:w\in W,\,\,i\in I\}$ be the corresponding root system; let $\Phi^{+}$ and $\Phi^{-}$ denote the sets of positive roots and negative roots, respectively. We have $\mathbb{R}\beta\cap\Phi=\{\pm\beta\}$ for each $\beta\in\Phi$ .

To each root $\beta=w\alpha_{i}$ , we associate a reflection $r_{\beta}=ws_{i}w^{-1}\in T$ ; this is well defined in the sense that it depends only on $\beta$ and not on the particular choices of $w$ and $\alpha_{i}$ . The map $\beta\mapsto r_{\beta}$ is a bijection from $\Phi^{+}$ to $T$ . We have $r_{\beta}=r_{-\beta}$ for all $\beta\in\Phi$ .

The action of $r_{\beta}$ on $V$ under the standard geometric representation is given by the formula

$$ r_{\beta}\gamma=\gamma-2B(\gamma,\beta)\beta. $$

For each reflection $t\in T$ , let $\beta_{t}$ denote the unique positive root such that $r_{\beta_{t}}=t$ . Then, for every $w\in W$ , we have

$$ \mathrm{Inv}(w)=\{t\in T:w\beta_{t}\in\Phi^{-}\}. $$

Equivalently, the half-space $H^{+}_{\beta_{t}}$ is equal to the set of all $w\in W$ that do not have $t$ as a right inversion. If $i_{M}\cdots i_{1}$ is reduced word for $w$ , then

$$ \{\alpha_{i_{1}},s_{i_{2}}\alpha_{i_{1}},s_{i_{3}}s_{i_{2}}\alpha_{i_{1}},\ldots,s_{i_{M}}\cdots s_{i_{3}}s_{i_{2}}\alpha_{i_{1}}\}=\{\beta_{t}:t\in\mathrm{Inv}(w)\}. $$

If $W$ is a finite Coxeter group, then we denote the long element of $W$ (the unique element of maximum length) by $w_{\circ}$ . It is known that $w_{\circ}$ is an involution and that $w_{\circ}\Phi^{+}=\Phi^{-}$ .

Recall that for $J\subseteq I$ , the (standard) parabolic subgroup $W_{J}$ is the subgroup of $W$ generated by $\{s_{i}:i\in J\}$ . Also recall that $(W_{J},\{s_{i}:i\in J\})$ is a Coxeter system. Let $V_{J}=\mathbb{R}^{J}\subseteq V$ denote the root space of $W_{J}$ , and let $\Phi_{J}=\{w\alpha_{i}:w\in W_{J},\,\,i\in J\}\subseteq V_{J}$ denote the root system of $W_{J}$ . By [11, Theorem 3.3], we have $\Phi_{J}=\Phi\cap V_{J}$ .

The irreducible factors of $W$ are the parabolic subgroups $W_{J_{1}},\ldots,W_{J_{k}}$ , where $J_{1},\ldots,J_{k}\subseteq I$ are the vertex sets of the connected components of the Coxeter graph $\Gamma_{W}$ . We have the direct product decomposition $W\cong W_{J_{1}}\times\cdots\times W_{J_{k}}$ . We say that $W$ is irreducible if $\Gamma_{W}$ is connected.

#### Remark 2.2.

It is straightforward to see that a Coxeter group is futuristic if and only if all of its irreducible factors are futuristic.

Let $\beta,\beta^{\prime}\in\Phi$ . We say $\beta$ dominates $\beta^{\prime}$ , written $\beta\mathrel{\mathsf{dom}}\beta^{\prime}$ , if $H_{\beta}^{+}\supseteq H_{\beta^{\prime}}^{+}$ . We say $\beta$ is small if $\beta\in\Phi^{+}$ and $\beta$ does not dominate any other positive root.

#### Remark 2.3.

Brink and Howlett [4] defined the dominance relation only for positive roots, but many of our results become easier to state if the relation is extended to all roots as above. The use of the word small comes from Björner and Brenti [2, Chapter 4.7].

Note that if $\beta\mathrel{\mathsf{dom}}\beta^{\prime}$ , then $-\beta^{\prime}\mathrel{\mathsf{dom}}-\beta$ and $u\beta\mathrel{\mathsf{dom}}u\beta^{\prime}$ for all $u\in W$ .

#### Proposition 2.4 ([2, Theorem 4.7.6]).

The set of small roots is the smallest set $\Sigma\subseteq\Phi^{+}$ that satisfies the following properties:

- (i) All simple roots are in $\Sigma$ .

- (ii) For $i\in I$ and $\gamma\in\Sigma\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}$ , if $0>B(\gamma,\alpha_{i})>-1$ , then $s_{i}\gamma\in\Sigma$ .

Moreover, the set of small roots is finite.

#### Corollary 2.5.

Let $\Sigma$ denote the set of small roots of $W$ . For $J\subseteq I$ , the set of small roots of the parabolic subgroup $W_{J}$ is $\Sigma\cap V_{J}$ .

## 3. Basics of Bender–Knuth Billiards

In this section, we establish more terminology and collect important facts concerning our general Bender–Knuth billiards systems.

### 3.1. Separators

As before, $(W,S)$ is a Coxeter system, and $S=\{s_{i}:i\in I\}$ , where $I$ is a finite index set. Fix a nonempty convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ .

In Section 1.2, we stated that a noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle $\tau_{i}$ cannot move an element “strictly away from” the convex set $\mathscr{L}$ . It is now time to formalize that observation. We define a separator for an element $u\in W$ to be an element of the set

$$ \mathrm{Sep}(u)=\{\beta\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L}):u\beta\in\Phi^{-}\}\subseteq\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L}). $$

(Note that $\mathrm{Sep}(u)$ depends on the convex set $\mathscr{L}$ .) The separators for $u$ correspond to (oriented) hyperplanes of the Coxeter arrangement that separate $\mathbb{B}u$ from $\mathbb{B}\mathscr{L}$ . Notice that since $\mathscr{L}$ is convex, we have $u\in\mathscr{L}$ if and only if $\mathrm{Sep}(u)=\varnothing$ .

#### Lemma 3.1.

Let $u\in W$ and $i\in I$ . Then $\mathrm{Sep}(\tau_{i}(u))\subseteq\mathrm{Sep}(u)$ . In fact,

$$ \displaystyle\tau_{i}(u)=\begin{cases}s_{i}u&\mbox{if $\mathrm{Sep}(s_{i}u)\subseteq\mathrm{Sep}(u)$;}\\
u&\mbox{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

#### Proof.

A root $\gamma$ satisfies $\gamma\in\Phi^{+}$ and $s_{i}\gamma\in\Phi^{-}$ if and only if $\gamma=\beta_{s_{i}}=\alpha_{i}$ . Also, by the definition of separators,

$$ \mathrm{Sep}(s_{i}u)\setminus\mathrm{Sep}(u)=\{\beta\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L}):s_{i}u\beta\in\Phi^{-}\text{ and }u\beta\in\Phi^{+}\}. $$

This set is $\{u^{-1}\alpha_{i}\}$ if $u^{-1}\alpha_{i}\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ and is $\varnothing$ otherwise. The lemma now follows from the definition of $\tau_{i}$ (Definition 1.2). ∎

One important consequence of Lemma 3.1 is that $\mathrm{Sep}(u_{0})=\mathrm{Sep}(u_{1})=\mathrm{Sep}(u_{2})=\cdots$ for any periodic billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ .

#### Example 3.2.

This example is a continuation of Example 1.3. Let $\mathscr{L}\subseteq\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ be a convex set. As before, there is an associated partial order $\leq_{\mathscr{L}}$ on $[n+1]$ . For each $u\in\mathfrak{S}_{n+1}$ , we have $e_{i}-e_{j}\in\mathrm{Sep}(u)$ if and only if $i\leq_{\mathscr{L}}j$ and $u(i)>u(j)$ . In other words, if we think of $u$ as a labeling of the poset $([n+1],\leq_{\mathscr{L}})$ , then the separators for $u$ correspond to the pairs of comparable elements whose labels are “in the wrong order”. Lemma 3.1 says that applying a noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle cannot create any new such pairs.

#### Lemma 3.3.

For every $u\in W$ , the set $\mathrm{Sep}(u)$ is finite.

#### Proof.

Fix some $w\in\mathscr{L}$ . For every $\beta\in\mathrm{Sep}(u)$ , we have $w\beta\in\Phi^{+}$ and $u\beta\in\Phi^{-}$ . Writing $u\beta=(uw^{-1})(w\beta)=(uw^{-1})\beta_{r_{w\beta}}$ , we see that $r_{w\beta}$ is a right inversion of $uw^{-1}$ . It follows that ${|\mathrm{Sep}(u)|\leq|\mathrm{Inv}(uw^{-1})|=\ell(uw^{-1})<\infty}$ . ∎

Recall that if $\mathsf{w}=i_{M}\cdots i_{1}$ is a word, then $\tau_{\mathsf{w}}$ denotes the composition $\tau_{i_{M}}\cdots\tau_{i_{1}}$ .

#### Lemma 3.4.

Let $w\in W$ , and let $\mathsf{w}$ be a reduced word for $w$ . Then

$$ \mathrm{Sep}(\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u))\subseteq\mathrm{Sep}(w^{-1}\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u)) $$

for all $u\in W$ .

#### Proof.

We proceed by induction on $M=\ell(w)$ . The base case $M=0$ is trivial, so assume that $M>0$ . Write $\mathsf{w}=i_{M}\cdots i_{1}$ . Let $\mathsf{w}^{\prime}=i_{M-1}\cdots i_{1}$ be the word obtained by deleting the leftmost letter of $\mathsf{w}$ , and let $w^{\prime}=s_{i_{M}}w\in W$ be the element of $W$ represented by the word $\mathsf{w}^{\prime}$ . Then $\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u)=\tau_{i_{M}}(\tau_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u))$ .

First, suppose that $\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u)=s_{i_{M}}\tau_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u)$ . Then $(w^{\prime})^{-1}\tau_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u)=w^{-1}\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u)$ . Hence, by Lemma 3.1 and the inductive hypothesis, we have

$$ \mathrm{Sep}(\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u))\subseteq\mathrm{Sep}(\tau_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u))\subseteq\mathrm{Sep}((w^{\prime})^{-1}\tau_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u))=\mathrm{Sep}(w^{-1}\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u)), $$

as desired.

Next, suppose that $\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u)=\tau_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u)$ . Let $v=\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u)=\tau_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u)$ . We wish to prove that

$$ {\mathrm{Sep}(v)\subseteq\mathrm{Sep}(w^{-1}v)}. $$

Choose any $\beta\in\mathrm{Sep}(v)$ ; we will show that $\beta\in\mathrm{Sep}(w^{-1}v)$ , i.e., that $w^{-1}v\beta\in\Phi^{-}$ . Recall that

$$ s_{i_{M}}v\beta=v\beta-2B(v\beta,\alpha_{i_{M}})\alpha_{i_{M}}. $$

We now consider two cases.

Case 1. Assume $B(v\beta,\alpha_{i_{M}})\geq 0$ . Then applying $(w^{\prime})^{-1}$ to each side of (12) yields

$$ w^{-1}v\beta=(w^{\prime})^{-1}v\beta-2B(v\beta,\alpha_{i_{M}})(w^{\prime})^{-1}\alpha_{i_{M}}. $$

By the inductive hypothesis, we have $\beta\in\mathrm{Sep}((w^{\prime})^{-1}v)$ , so $(w^{\prime})^{-1}v\beta\in\Phi^{-}$ . Moreover, $s_{i_{M}}$ is not a right inversion of $(w^{\prime})^{-1}$ , so by (10), we have $(w^{\prime})^{-1}\alpha_{i_{M}}\in\Phi^{+}$ . It follows that $w^{-1}v\beta\in\Phi^{-}$ , as desired.

Case 2. Assume $B(v\beta,\alpha_{i_{M}})<0$ . We will prove that $v^{-1}s_{i_{M}}v\beta\in\mathrm{Sep}((w^{\prime})^{-1}v)$ ; this will imply that

$$ w^{-1}v\beta=(w^{\prime})^{-1}v(v^{-1}s_{i_{M}}v\beta)\in\Phi^{-}, $$

as desired. Our inductive hypothesis tells us that $\mathrm{Sep}(v)\subseteq\mathrm{Sep}((w^{\prime})^{-1}v)$ , so it suffices to show that $v^{-1}s_{i_{M}}v\beta\in\mathrm{Sep}(v)$ ; that is, we want to show that $v^{-1}s_{i_{M}}v\beta\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ and $v(v^{-1}s_{i_{M}}v)\beta\in\Phi^{-}$ .

Applying $v^{-1}$ to each side of (12) yields

$$ v^{-1}s_{i_{M}}v\beta=\beta-2B(v\beta,\alpha_{i_{M}})v^{-1}\alpha_{i_{M}}. $$

We know that $\beta\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ . Since $\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u)=\tau_{\mathsf{w}^{\prime}}(u)=v$ , we also have $v^{-1}\alpha_{i_{M}}\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ . Because $\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ is closed, this implies that $v^{-1}s_{i_{M}}v\beta\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ . Since $-\beta\not\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ , we also know that $-\beta\neq v^{-1}\alpha_{i_{M}}$ , so $v\beta\neq-\alpha_{i_{M}}$ . Since $v\beta\in\Phi^{-}\setminus\{-\alpha_{i_{M}}\}$ , we also conclude that $v(v^{-1}s_{i_{M}}v)\beta=s_{i_{M}}v\beta\in\Phi^{-}$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.5.

Lemma 3.4 is equivalent to the statement that the function $W\to W$ given by $u\mapsto w^{-1}\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(u)$ is idempotent. It is unclear whether this formulation is useful.

### 3.2. Strata

It will be useful to classify the elements of $W$ by their separators. We define the stratum corresponding to a finite subset $R\subseteq\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ to be the set

$$ \mathrm{Str}(R)=\{u\in W:\mathrm{Sep}(u)=R\}. $$

Note that the nonempty strata form a partition of the set $W$ . By Lemma 3.1, any periodic billiards trajectory is contained in a single stratum. The stratum corresponding to the empty set is $\mathscr{L}$ itself; we call the other nonempty strata the proper strata.

Strata have the following geometric interpretation. Recall that the hyperplanes $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ for $\beta\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ are called one-way mirrors (see Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4, where one-way mirrors are drawn as yellow-and-red lines or curves). These hyperplanes form a subarrangement $\mathcal{H}^{\mathscr{L}}_{W}$ of the Coxeter arrangement $\mathcal{H}_{W}$ . The nonempty strata correspond to the intersections of the regions of $\mathcal{H}^{\mathscr{L}}_{W}$ with the Tits cone.

#### Lemma 3.6.

If $\mathscr{L}$ is finite, then $|\mathrm{Str}(R)|\leq 2^{|\Phi\setminus(\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})\cup(-\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})))|}$ for all $R\subseteq\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ .

#### Proof.

Fix an arbitrary $v\in\mathrm{Str}(R)$ . Each element $u\in\mathrm{Str}(R)$ is uniquely determined by the set of hyperplanes in the Coxeter arrangement $\mathcal{H}_{W}$ that separate $\mathbb{B}v$ from $\mathbb{B}u$ . Each such hyperplane must be of the form $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ for some root $\beta$ in the finite set $\Phi\setminus(\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})\cup(-\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})))$ . ∎

Every proper stratum has at least one transmitting root.

By the minimality of $\ell(vw^{-1})$ , we have that $s_{i}w\not\in\mathrm{Str}(R)$ , so $\mathrm{Sep}(s_{i}w)\neq\mathrm{Sep}(w)$ . ### 3.3. Conjugate Coxeter Elements

Consider the Coxeter graph $\Gamma_{W}$ of $W$ . An acyclic orientation of $\Gamma_{W}$ is a directed graph with no directed cycles that is obtained by orienting each edge of $\Gamma_{W}$ . A sink (respectively, source) of an acyclic orientation is a vertex with out-degree (respectively, in-degree) $0$ . If $i$ is a source or a sink of $\Gamma_{W}$ , then we can flip $i$ by reversing the orientations of all edges incident to $i$ ; the result is a new acyclic orientation of $\Gamma_{W}$ . We say two acyclic orientations of $\Gamma_{W}$ are flip equivalent if one can be obtained from the other via a sequence of flips.

Let $c$ be a Coxeter element of $W$ . Let us direct the edge between two adjacent vertices $i$ and $i^{\prime}$ in $\Gamma_{W}$ from $i$ to $i^{\prime}$ if $i$ appears to the right of $i^{\prime}$ in some (equivalently, every) reduced word for $c$ . Doing this for all edges in $\Gamma_{W}$ yields an acyclic orientation $\mathrm{ao}(c)$ of $\Gamma_{W}$ .

The map $\mathrm{ao}$ is a bijection from the set of Coxeter elements of $W$ to the set of acyclic orientations of $\Gamma_{W}$ . Moreover, it is known [10, Theorem 1.15] that two Coxeter elements $c$ and $c^{\prime}$ are conjugate in $W$ if and only if $\mathrm{ao}(c)$ and $\mathrm{ao}(c^{\prime})$ are flip equivalent.

#### Proposition 3.12.

Let $c$ and $c^{\prime}$ be Coxeter elements of $W$ that are conjugate to each other. Then $c$ is futuristic if and only if $c^{\prime}$ is futuristic.

#### Proof.

According to [10, Theorem 1.15], the acyclic orientations $\mathrm{ao}(c)$ and $\mathrm{ao}(c^{\prime})$ are flip equivalent. Hence, we may assume that $\mathrm{ao}(c^{\prime})$ is obtained from $\mathrm{ao}(c)$ via a single flip from a source to a sink. That is, there is a reduced word $i_{n}i_{n-1}\cdots i_{1}$ for $c$ such that $i_{n-1}\cdots i_{1}i_{n}$ is a reduced word for $c^{\prime}$ .

Fix an arbitrary nonempty convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ . Suppose $c$ is futuristic. Let $u\in W$ be a periodic point of $\mathrm{Pro}_{c^{\prime}}$ . We have that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}\circ\tau_{i_{n}}=\tau_{i_{n}}\circ\mathrm{Pro}_{c^{\prime}}$ , so $\tau_{i_{n}}(u)$ must be a periodic point of $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}$ . Since $c$ is futuristic, this implies that $\tau_{i_{n}}(u)\in\mathscr{L}$ . Because $u$ is a periodic point of $\mathrm{Pro}_{c^{\prime}}$ , it can be obtained by applying a sequence of noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles to $\tau_{i_{n}}(u)$ . Hence, $u\in\mathscr{L}$ . This proves that $c^{\prime}$ is futuristic.

We have shown that if $c$ is futuristic, then $c^{\prime}$ is futuristic. A similar argument proves the other direction. ∎

It is well known that all acyclic orientations of a forest are flip equivalent, so we immediately obtain the following corollary.

#### Corollary 3.13.

If the Coxeter graph of a Coxeter group $W$ is a forest, then $W$ is either futuristic or ancient.

### 3.4. Futuristicity is Hereditary

We now prove Proposition 1.12, which states that the class of futuristic Coxeter groups and the class of non-ancient Coxeter groups are hereditary in the sense that they are closed under taking standard parabolic subgroups. In fact, these results are immediate corollaries of the following stronger proposition.

#### Proposition 3.14.

Let $J\subseteq I$ . Let $c$ be a Coxeter element of $W$ , and let $c^{\prime}$ be a Coxeter element of the standard parabolic subgroup $W_{J}$ such that there exists a reduced word for $c$ that contains a reduced word for $c^{\prime}$ as a subword. If $c$ is futuristic, then $c^{\prime}$ is also futuristic.

#### Proof.

Assume that $c$ is futuristic; we will show that $c^{\prime}$ is futuristic. Let $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W_{J}$ be a nonempty convex set; we will show that every periodic point of $\mathrm{Pro}_{c^{\prime}}$ lies in $\mathscr{L}$ .

Note that $W_{J}$ is precisely the set of elements of $W$ with no right inversions in $W\setminus W_{J}$ , so $W_{J}$ is a convex subset of $W$ , with $\mathrm{R}(W_{J})=\Phi^{+}\setminus\Phi_{J}$ . Now, write $\mathrm{R}_{J}(\mathscr{L})=\{\beta\in\Phi_{J}:\mathscr{L}\subseteq H_{\beta}^{+}\}$ . We have

$$ \mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})\cap\Phi_{J}=\mathrm{R}_{J}(\mathscr{L}), $$

and the inclusion $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W_{J}$ gives $\Phi^{+}\setminus\Phi_{J}\subseteq\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ . At the same time, we have $w\beta\in\Phi^{-}$ for all $w\in\mathscr{L}$ and $\beta\in\Phi^{-}\setminus\Phi_{J}$ , so $\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ is disjoint from $\Phi^{-}\setminus\Phi_{J}$ . Putting this all together yields

$$ \mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})=\mathrm{R}_{J}(\mathscr{L})\cup(\Phi^{+}\setminus\Phi_{J}). $$

Moreover, $\mathscr{L}$ is the intersection of the half-spaces $H_{\beta}^{+}$ for $\beta\in\mathrm{R}_{J}(\mathscr{L})\cup(\Phi^{+}\setminus\Phi_{J})$ , so $\mathscr{L}$ is convex as a subset of $W$ .

For $i\in I$ , let $\tau_{i}\colon W\to W$ denote the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle on $W$ that is defined with respect to $\mathscr{L}$ . For $i\in J$ , let $\tau^{J}_{i}\colon W_{J}\to W_{J}$ denote the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle on $W_{J}$ that is defined with respect to $\mathscr{L}$ .

We claim that for all $i\in J$ , the restriction of $\tau_{i}$ to $W_{J}$ is $\tau_{i}^{J}$ . Moreover, we claim that for all $i\in I\setminus J$ , the restriction of $\tau_{i}$ to $W_{J}$ is the identity function on $W_{J}$ . Let $i\in I$ and $u\in W_{J}$ . Then $\tau_{i}(u)=u$ if and only if $u^{-1}\alpha_{i}\in\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ . By (14), this holds if and only if $u^{-1}\alpha_{i}\in\mathrm{R}_{J}(\mathscr{L})$ or $i\not\in J$ ; this proves both claims.

It follows that the restriction of $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}$ to $W_{J}$ is $\mathrm{Pro}_{c^{\prime}}$ . Since $c$ is futuristic, every periodic point of $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}$ lies in $\mathscr{L}$ . Hence, every periodic point of $\mathrm{Pro}_{c^{\prime}}$ lies in $\mathscr{L}$ , as desired. ∎

### 3.5. Folding

There is a common technique known as folding that can be used to obtain new Coxeter groups from old ones [31]. In this subsection, we discuss this technique and its relation to Bender–Knuth billiards. We were not able to find a discussion of folding root systems in the literature at the level of generality that we present here, so we will prove all of the relevant statements. However, on the level of Coxeter groups, these foldings are discussed in [12, 26].

Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system whose simple reflections are indexed by a finite index set $I$ , and let $\sigma\colon I\to I$ be an automorphism of the Coxeter graph $\Gamma_{W}$ such that each orbit (i.e., cycle) of $\sigma$ is an independent set (i.e., a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices). Let $I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ be the set of orbits of $\sigma$ .55 5 The symbol w is pronounced “fold”. Consider a symbol $s_{\mathfrak{o}}$ for each orbit $\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . Let $S^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}=\{s_{\mathfrak{o}}:\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}\}$ , and let $(W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}},S^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})$ be the Coxeter system such that for all $\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , the order $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})$ of $s_{\mathfrak{o}}s_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}$ in $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ is equal to the order of $\prod_{i\in\mathfrak{o}}s_{i}\prod_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}s_{i^{\prime}}$ in $W$ . Observe that there is a group homomorphism $\iota\colon W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}\to W$ determined by $\iota(s_{\mathfrak{o}})=\prod_{i\in\mathfrak{o}}s_{i}$ . (The map $\iota$ is actually injective [26], but we will not need this.) We call $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ a folding of $W$ . We also say $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ is obtained from $W$ by folding along $\sigma$ .

#### Example 3.15.

The Coxeter graph of the affine Coxeter group $\widetilde{E}_{6}$ is

$$ \begin{array}[]{l}\includegraphics[height=40.11848pt]{BKTogglesPIC25}\end{array}\,\,. $$

We have shaded in red the orbits of a Coxeter graph automorphism of order 2. By folding along this automorphism, we obtain the affine Coxeter group $\widetilde{F}_{4}$ , whose Coxeter graph is

$$ \includegraphics[height=10.6129pt]{BKTogglesPIC22}\,\,. $$

The Coxeter graph of the affine Coxeter group $\widetilde{E}_{7}$ is

$$ \begin{array}[]{l}\includegraphics[height=40.11848pt]{BKTogglesPIC26}\end{array}\,\,. $$

As in the case of $\widetilde{E}_{6}$ , we have shaded in red the orbits of a Coxeter graph automorphism of order 2. By folding along this automorphism, we again obtain $\widetilde{F}_{4}$ .

For each orbit $\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , let us fix a particular index $i_{\mathfrak{o}}\in\mathfrak{o}$ . For $\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , let $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})$ denote the number of edges in $\Gamma_{W}$ of the form $\{i_{\mathfrak{o}},i^{\prime}\}$ for $i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}$ . Let $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})$ be the multiset of labels of the form $m(i_{\mathfrak{o}},i^{\prime})$ with $i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}$ and $m(i_{\mathfrak{o}},i^{\prime})\geq 3$ , where the multiplicity of a label $a$ in $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})$ is equal to ${|\{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}:m(i_{\mathfrak{o}},i^{\prime})=a\}|}$ . (Because $\sigma$ is a Coxeter graph automorphism, neither $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})$ nor $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})$ depends on the choice of $i_{\mathfrak{o}}$ .) Thus, $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})$ is the cardinality of $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})$ , counted with multiplicity. In particular, if $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=0$ (i.e., $\mathfrak{o}\cup\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}$ is an independent set in $\Gamma_{W}$ ), then $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})$ is empty. The following lemma allows us to determine the label $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})$ of the edge between $\mathfrak{o}$ and $\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}$ in $\Gamma_{W^{\raisebox{0.43054pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}}$ from the tuples $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})$ and $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})$ .

#### Lemma 3.16.

Let $\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}$ be distinct orbits in $I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , and assume that $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})\leq\deg_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})$ .

- • If $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=0$ , then $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=2$ .

- • If $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=\deg_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=1$ , then $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\{m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})\}$ .

- • If $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=1$ and $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\{3,3\}$ , then $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=4$ .

- • If $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=1$ and $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\{3,3,3\}$ , then $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=6$ .

- • If $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=1<\deg_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})$ and $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})$ is not $\{3,3\}$ or $\{3,3,3\}$ , then $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\infty$ .

- • If $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})\geq 2$ , then $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\infty$ .

#### Proof.

By passing to the parabolic subgroup $W_{\mathfrak{o}\cup\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}$ , we may assume that $\mathfrak{o}\cup\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}=I$ .

It is immediate from the definitions that $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=2$ if $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=0$ .

Suppose that $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=1$ . The irreducible factors of $W$ are pairwise isomorphic Coxeter groups, and the Coxeter graph of each irreducible factor is a star graph whose edges all have the same label. To compute the order of $\prod_{i\in\mathfrak{o}}s_{i}\prod_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}s_{i^{\prime}}$ in $W$ , we compute the order after projecting to each irreducible factor, and we then take the least common multiple of the orders obtained this way (which will all be equal because the irreducible factors are isomorphic). We can check directly that this order is $a$ if $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\{a\}$ , is $4$ if $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\{3,3\}$ , is $6$ if $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\{3,3,3\}$ , and is $\infty$ otherwise.

Finally, suppose that $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})\geq 2$ . Let $\mathfrak{o}=\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\}$ and $\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}=\{i_{1}^{\prime},\ldots,i_{k^{\prime}}^{\prime}\}$ , and let $b\geq 1$ be an integer. Upon inspection, we find that it is impossible to apply a sequence of commutation moves to the word $(i_{1}\cdots i_{k}i_{1}^{\prime}\cdots i_{k^{\prime}}^{\prime})^{b}$ to obtain a word to which we can apply a nil move or a braid move that is not a commutation move. By Matsumoto’s theorem (Theorem 2.1), this implies that $(i_{1}\cdots i_{k}i_{1}^{\prime}\cdots i_{k^{\prime}}^{\prime})^{b}$ is a reduced word. Hence, $\prod_{i\in\mathfrak{o}}s_{i}\prod_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}s_{i^{\prime}}$ does not have order $b$ . As $b$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\infty$ . ∎

Let us now discuss how root systems interact with folding. Recall that when defining the bilinear form in (6), we had to choose a number $\mu_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}\geq 1$ whenever $m(i,i^{\prime})=\infty$ ; we now stress that, in this subsection, we will sometimes need to choose a value for $\mu_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}$ that is strictly greater than $1$ .

Let $V$ be the root space of $W$ , and let $B$ be a bilinear form on $V$ induced by $W$ . Let $V^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ be the root space of $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . Define a bilinear form $B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}\colon V^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}\times V^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}\to\mathbb{R}$ by setting

$$ B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}(\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}},\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}})=-\sqrt{\left(\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}B(\alpha_{i_{\mathfrak{o}}},\alpha_{i^{\prime}})\right)\left(\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{o}}B(\alpha_{i_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}},\alpha_{i})\right)}. $$

Because $\sigma$ is a Coxeter graph automorphism, we can equivalently write

$$ B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}(\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}},\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}})=\sqrt{\frac{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})}{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})}}\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}B(\alpha_{i_{\mathfrak{o}}},\alpha_{i^{\prime}})=\sqrt{\frac{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})}{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})}}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{o}}B(\alpha_{i_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}},\alpha_{i}). $$

It will be useful to keep in mind that

$$ \sqrt{\frac{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})}{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})}}=\sqrt{\frac{|\mathfrak{o}|}{|\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}|}} $$

(this is also a consequence of the fact that $\sigma$ is a Coxeter graph automorphism).

#### Lemma 3.17.

The bilinear form $B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ is induced by $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , and assume without loss of generality that $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})\leq\deg_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})$ . The proof follows from Lemma 3.16 and (16). For example, if $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})=1$ and $\mathrm{lab}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\{3,3,3\}$ , then

$$ B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}(\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}},\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}})=\sqrt{\frac{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})}{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})}}\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}B(\alpha_{i_{\mathfrak{o}}},\alpha_{i^{\prime}})=\sqrt{\frac{3}{1}}(-\cos(\pi/3))=-\cos(\pi/6), $$

and $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=6$ by Lemma 3.16. If $\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})\geq 2$ , then

$$ B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}(\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}},\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}})=\sqrt{\frac{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}}(\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})}{\deg_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}(\mathfrak{o})}}\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}B(\alpha_{i_{\mathfrak{o}}},\alpha_{i^{\prime}})\leq\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}B(\alpha_{i_{\mathfrak{o}}},\alpha_{i^{\prime}})\leq 2(-\cos(\pi/3))=-1, $$

and $m(\mathfrak{o},\mathfrak{o}^{\prime})=\infty$ by Lemma 3.16. Similar arguments handle the other cases. ∎

Lemma 3.17 allows us to consider the standard geometric representation of $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ defined with respect to $B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . Define the linear transformation $\omega\colon V\to V^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ by taking $\omega(\alpha_{i})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathfrak{o}|}}\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}}$ for all $\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ and all $i\in\mathfrak{o}$ . We claim that

$$ \omega(\iota(v)\beta)=v\omega(\beta) $$

for all $v\in W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ and $\beta\in V$ . It suffices to prove this when $\beta=\alpha_{i}$ is a simple root and $v=s_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}$ is a simple reflection. Let $\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ be the orbit containing $i$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\omega(\iota(s_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}})\alpha_{i}) \displaystyle=\omega\left(\alpha_{i}-\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}B(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i^{\prime}})\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathfrak{o}|}}\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}}-\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}B(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i^{\prime}})\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}|}}\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathfrak{o}|}}\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathfrak{o}|}}B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}(\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}},\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}})\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}, $$

where the last equality follows from (16) and (17). Because

$$ s_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}\omega(\alpha_{i})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathfrak{o}|}}s_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathfrak{o}|}}\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mathfrak{o}|}}B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}(\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}},\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}})\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}^{\prime}}, $$

this completes the proof of (18).

In what follows, we will write $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ for the root system of $W$ (defined with respect to $B$ ) and the root system of $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ (defined with respect to $B^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ ), respectively. A version of this lemma (without root systems) also appears as [12, Theorem 6.1(c)].

#### Lemma 3.18.

Let $\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , and let $i\in\mathfrak{o}$ . For $v\in W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , we have $v\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}}\in(\Phi^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})^{+}$ if and only if $\iota(v)\alpha_{i}\in\Phi^{+}$ .

#### Proof.

According to (18), we have $v\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}}=\sqrt{|\mathfrak{o}|}\omega(\iota(v)\alpha_{i})$ , so the proof follows from the fact that $\omega$ maps each simple root of $W$ to a positive scalar multiple of a simple root of $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . ∎

Let $\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ be a nonempty convex subset of $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , and let $\mathscr{L}$ be the convex hull of $\iota(\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})$ in $W$ . For $i\in I$ , let $\tau_{i}$ be the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle on $W$ defined with respect to $\mathscr{L}$ . For $\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , let $\tau_{\mathfrak{o}}$ be the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle on $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ defined with respect to $\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , and let $\overline{\tau}_{\mathfrak{o}}=\prod_{i\in\mathfrak{o}}\tau_{i}$ , where $\prod$ denotes composition. The order of the composition does not matter because $\mathfrak{o}$ is an independent set of $\Gamma_{W}$ .

#### Lemma 3.19.

For every $\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , we have $\iota\circ\tau_{\mathfrak{o}}=\overline{\tau}_{\mathfrak{o}}\circ\iota$ .

#### Proof.

Fix $\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ and $x\in W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . We wish to prove that $\iota(\tau_{\mathfrak{o}}(x))=\overline{\tau}_{\mathfrak{o}}(\iota(x))$ . To do so, it suffices to show that for each $i\in\mathfrak{o}$ , we have $\tau_{\mathfrak{o}}(x)=x$ if and only if $\tau_{i}(\iota(x))=\iota(x)$ .

Fix $i\in\mathfrak{o}$ . We have $\tau_{\mathfrak{o}}(x)=x$ if and only if $wx^{-1}\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}}\in(\Phi^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})^{+}$ for all $w\in\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . According to Lemma 3.18, this holds if and only if $\iota(w)(\iota(x)^{-1}\alpha_{i})\in\Phi^{+}$ for all $w\in\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . Because $\mathscr{L}$ is the convex hull of $\iota(\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})$ , it follows that $\tau_{\mathfrak{o}}(x)=x$ if and only if $z(\iota(x)^{-1}\alpha_{i})\in\Phi^{+}$ for all $z\in\mathscr{L}$ . This, in turn, holds if and only if $\tau_{i}(\iota(x))=\iota(x)$ . ∎

We are now prepared to prove Proposition 1.13, which states that a folding of a futuristic Coxeter group is futuristic. This result is immediate from the following stronger proposition. Note that if $c$ is a Coxeter element of $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , then $\iota(c)$ is a Coxeter element of $W$ .

#### Proposition 3.20.

Let $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ be a folding of $W$ , and let $c$ be a Coxeter element of $W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . If $\iota(c)$ is futuristic, then $c$ is futuristic.

#### Proof.

Preserve the notation from above. We prove the contrapositive. Suppose that $c$ is not futuristic. Then there exist a nonempty convex set $\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}\subseteq W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ and an element $u\in W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}\setminus\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ such that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{K}(u)=u$ for some integer $K\geq 1$ . Let $\mathscr{L}$ be the convex hull in $W$ of $\iota(\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})$ . It follows from Lemma 3.19 that $\iota\circ\mathrm{Pro}_{c}=\mathrm{Pro}_{\iota(c)}\circ\iota$ . Hence, $\mathrm{Pro}_{\iota(c)}^{K}(\iota(u))=\iota(\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{K}(u))=\iota(u)$ .

We need to show that $\iota(u)\not\in\mathscr{L}$ . Because $u\not\in\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , there exists $\beta\in\Phi^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ such that $u\beta\in(\Phi^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})^{-}$ and $w\beta\in(\Phi^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})^{+}$ for all $w\in\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . We can write $\beta=y\alpha_{\mathfrak{o}}$ for some $y\in W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ and $\mathfrak{o}\in I^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . Choose $i\in\mathfrak{o}$ . For each $v\in W^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ , we can use Lemma 3.18 to see that $v\beta\in(\Phi^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})^{+}$ if and only if $\iota(v)(\iota(y)\alpha_{i})\in\Phi^{+}$ . It follows that $\iota(u)(\iota(y)\alpha_{i})\in\Phi^{-}$ and that $\iota(w)(\iota(y)\alpha_{i})\in\Phi^{+}$ for all $w\in\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}}$ . Since $\mathscr{L}$ is the convex hull of $\iota(\mathscr{L}^{\raisebox{0.60275pt}{\resizebox{0}{32768}{\rotatebox{90.0}{{w}}}}})$ , we deduce that $\iota(u)\not\in\mathscr{L}$ . ∎

## 4. Finite Coxeter Groups

Throughout this section, we assume that the Coxeter group $W$ is finite.

The machinery developed in Section 3.1 allows us to painlessly finish the proofs of Theorems 1.22 and 1.24.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.22.

Let $\mathsf{w}_{\circ}$ be a reduced word for $w_{\circ}$ . Let $u\in W$ , and assume for the sake of contradiction that $\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}(u)\not\in\mathscr{L}$ . Then there is some $\beta\in\mathrm{Sep}(\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}(u))$ . According to Lemma 3.4, we have $\beta\in\mathrm{Sep}(w_{\circ}^{-1}\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}(u))$ . But then the roots $\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}(u)\beta$ and $w_{\circ}^{-1}\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}(u)\beta$ are both negative, which contradicts the fact that $w_{\circ}\Phi^{+}=\Phi^{-}$ (recall that $w_{\circ}^{-1}=w_{\circ}$ ). ∎

In the following proof, recall the commutation equivalence relation $\equiv$ defined in Section 2.

#### Proof of Corollary 1.24.

Let $\mathsf{c}$ be a reduced word for the Coxeter element $c$ . It follows from [29, Corollary 4.1] that there is a reduced word $\mathsf{w}_{\circ}$ for $w_{\circ}$ such that $\mathsf{c}^{\mathrm{M}(c)}\equiv\mathsf{y}\mathsf{w}_{\circ}$ for some word $\mathsf{y}$ . Appealing to Theorem 1.22, we find that

$$ \mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{\mathrm{M}(c)}(W)=\tau_{\mathsf{y}}(\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}(W))=\tau_{\mathsf{y}}(\mathscr{L})=\mathscr{L}.\qed $$

In the remainder of this section, we provide a (slightly informal) discussion of how one can compute $\mathrm{M}(c)$ explicitly.

Let $\mathsf{x}$ be a word. Let $i\in I$ , and let $p_{i}(\mathsf{x})$ be the number of occurrences of $i$ in $\mathsf{x}$ . For $1\leq k\leq p_{i}(\mathsf{x})$ , let $i^{(k)}$ be the $k$ -th occurrence of $i$ in $\mathsf{x}$ (counted from the right). It will be convenient to view $i^{(1)},\ldots,i^{(p_{i}(\mathsf{x}))}$ as distinct entities. The heap of $\mathsf{x}$ is a certain poset whose elements are the letters in $\mathsf{x}$ (which are seen as distinct from one another, even if they are equal as elements of $I$ ). The order relation is defined so that if $i_{1}^{(k_{1})}$ and $i_{2}^{(k_{2})}$ are two letters, then $i_{1}^{(k_{1})}<i_{2}^{(k_{2})}$ if and only if $i_{1}^{(k_{1})}$ appears to the right of $i_{2}^{(k_{2})}$ in every word that is commutation equivalent to $\mathsf{x}$ . Two words are commutation equivalent if and only if they have the same heap. The Hasse diagram of the heap of $\mathsf{x}$ , which we denote by $\mathrm{Heap}(\mathsf{x})$ , is called a combinatorial AR quiver [33]. We will draw $\mathrm{Heap}(\mathsf{x})$ sideways so that larger letters appear to the left of smaller letters.66 6 It is typical to draw $\mathrm{Heap}(\mathsf{x})$ with larger letters to the right of smaller letters, but we have adopted the opposite convention in order to match our equally unorthodox convention for writing words.

There is an involution $\psi\colon I\to I$ given by $s_{\psi(i)}=w_{\circ}s_{i}w_{\circ}$ . We can extend $\psi$ to an involution on the set of words over $I$ by letting $\psi(i_{M}\cdots i_{1})=\psi(i_{M})\cdots\psi(i_{1})$ .

Recall that the Coxeter number of $W$ is the quantity $h=|\Phi|/|S|$ . Let $\mathsf{c}$ be a reduced word for a Coxeter element $c$ . It is known that $\mathrm{M}(c)\leq h$ . In fact, it follows from [33, Lemma 2.6.5] that

$$ \mathsf{c}^{h}\equiv\psi(\mathsf{sort}_{\mathsf{c}}(w_{\circ}))\mathsf{sort}_{\mathsf{c}}(w_{\circ}), $$

where $\mathsf{sort}_{\mathsf{c}}(w_{\circ})$ is a special reduced word called the $\mathsf{c}$ -sorting word for $w_{\circ}$ (see [28]). One can compute $\mathsf{sort}_{\mathsf{c}}(w_{\circ})$ by drawing the combinatorial AR quiver $\mathrm{Heap}(\mathsf{c}^{h})$ and then “cutting” the diagram in half so that the left side can be obtained by applying $\psi$ to the right side. Then $\mathrm{M}(c)$ is the smallest positive integer $k$ such that the right side fits inside of $\mathrm{Heap}(\mathsf{c}^{k})$ .

#### Example 4.1.

Suppose that $W=\mathfrak{S}_{7}$ , and let $s_{i}=(i\,\,i+1)$ . The Coxeter number of $\mathfrak{S}_{7}$ is $h=7$ . Consider the word $\mathsf{c}=213456$ , and let $c=s_{2}s_{1}s_{3}s_{4}s_{5}s_{6}$ be the Coxeter element represented by $\mathsf{c}$ . Figure 6 shows the combinatorial AR quiver of $\mathsf{c}^{7}$ ; it is formed by placing $7$ copies of $\mathrm{Heap}(\mathsf{c})$ (indicated by bands shaded in yellow) in a row and adding (black) edges as appropriate.

The involution $\psi\colon I\to I$ is given by $\psi(i)=7-i$ . The thick black-and-blue piecewise linear curve in Figure 6 cuts the diagram into two pieces such that the piece on the left side of the cut can be obtained by applying $\psi$ to the piece on the right side of the cut. Thus, the piece on the right side of the cut is $\mathrm{Heap}(\mathsf{sort}_{\mathsf{c}}(w_{\circ}))$ . The piece on the right of the cut uses letters from $5$ different yellow bands, so $\mathrm{M}(c)=5$ .
