## 5. Affine Coxeter Groups

This section discusses general results about Bender–Knuth billiards in affine Coxeter groups. We will use these results to prove Theorem 1.15, which states that the affine Coxeter groups of types $\widetilde{A}$ , $\widetilde{C}$ , and $\widetilde{G}_{2}$ are futuristic.

### 5.1. Affine Coxeter Groups

Preserve the notation from Section 2, and assume in addition that the Coxeter system $(W,S)$ is affine. This means that the associated bilinear form $B\colon V\times V\to\mathbb{R}$ is positive semidefinite but not positive definite. We will also assume that $W$ is irreducible. Let

$$ V^{W}=\{\gamma\in V:\text{$u\gamma=\gamma$ for all $u\in W$}\} $$

be the space of $W$ -invariant vectors in $V$ . Equivalently, $V^{W}$ is the kernel of $B$ . The space $V^{W}$ is $1$ -dimensional, and there exists $\delta\in V^{W}$ whose coefficients in the basis of simple roots are all positive. We call $\delta$ the imaginary root, though the reader should keep in mind that it is not a root of $W$ .

Let $\overline{V}=V/V^{W}$ , and let $\pi\colon V\to\overline{V}$ be the quotient map. Then $\overline{V}$ is a $W$ -module, and the form $B$ descends to a $W$ -invariant real inner product $\overline{B}\colon\overline{V}\times\overline{V}\to\mathbb{R}$ . Unlike $V$ , the $W$ -module $\overline{V}$ is not faithful; that is, the homomorphism $\rho_{\overline{V}}\colon W\to\mathrm{GL}(\overline{V})$ is not injective. Let $\overline{W}$ be the quotient group $W/\ker(\rho_{\overline{V}})$ , and let $\pi\colon W\to\overline{W}$ be the quotient map. (It is a slight abuse of notation to use the letter $\pi$ to refer to two different quotient maps, but it will always be clear from context which is meant.) It is well known that $\overline{W}$ is a finite Coxeter group.

We will make use of the following result due to Speyer. (As noted in Speyer’s article, this result was already proved for affine Coxeter groups in [14, 21].)

#### Theorem 5.1 ([29, Theorem 1]).

Let $W$ be an infinite irreducible Coxeter group, and let $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ be an ordering of the index set $I$ . For every $K\geq 1$ , the word $(i_{n}\cdots i_{1})^{K}$ is reduced.

To prove that the affine Coxeter groups of type $\widetilde{A}$ are futuristic, we will use the following theorem, whose proof is type-uniform.

#### Theorem 5.2.

Let $W$ be an irreducible affine Coxeter group. Let $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ be a nonempty convex set, let $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ be an ordering of the index set $I$ , and let $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ be a corresponding periodic billiards trajectory that is contained within a single proper stratum $\mathrm{Str}(R)$ . Let $\beta$ be a transmitting root of $\mathrm{Str}(R)$ . If $j$ is a positive integer such that $u_{j}=u_{j-1}$ , then $B(u_{j-1}\beta,\alpha_{i_{j}})=0$ .

#### Proof.

It may help to keep the following geometric intuition in mind. As in Figure 1, we can think of the Bender–Knuth billiards process as taking place within the Tits cone ${\mathbb{B}W}$ , or, equivalently, in the positive projectivization $\mathbb{P}({\mathbb{B}W})=({\mathbb{B}W}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ , which has the structure of an affine Euclidean space. By Lemma 3.10, the billiards trajectory can never reflect off of a one-way mirror that forms an obtuse angle with the hyperplane $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ . Thus, if the billiards trajectory is ever moving toward the hyperplane $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ , it can never be redirected to move away from $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ . Since the billiards trajectory is periodic, the only possibility is that it always moves parallel to $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ and hits only one-way mirrors that are orthogonal to $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ . In other words, if $u_{j}=u_{j-1}$ , then $B(u_{j-1}\beta,\alpha_{i_{j}})=0$ .

Of course, the billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ is really a sequence of elements of $W$ , rather than an actual piecewise linear path inside $\mathbb{P}({\mathbb{B}W})$ . (But see Sections 11 and 12.4.) So, in order to turn our geometric intuition into a rigorous proof, we must formalize the notions of “moving toward” and “moving away from” $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ . We can do so as follows.

Consider the Coxeter element $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ . There is an integer $K\geq 1$ such that ${\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{K}(u_{0})=u_{0}}$ and $\pi(c)^{K}=\mathbbm{1}$ . For $j\geq 1$ , define

$$ \lambda_{j}=\begin{cases}2B(u_{j-1}\beta,\alpha_{i_{j}})&\mbox{if $u_{j}=u_{j-1}$;}\\
0&\mbox{if $u_{j}=s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}$.}\end{cases} $$

By Lemma 3.10, we have $\lambda_{j}\geq 0$ for all $j$ , and we wish to prove that $\lambda_{j}=0$ for all $j$ . Observe that we have defined $\lambda_{j}$ in such a way that

$$ u_{j}\beta=s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}\beta+\lambda_{j}\alpha_{i_{j}}. $$

For $j\geq 0$ , define

$$ c_{j}=s_{i_{j+n}}\cdots s_{i_{j+2}}s_{i_{j+1}}\in W\quad\text{and}\quad\gamma_{j}=c_{j}^{K}u_{j}\beta-u_{j}\beta\in V. $$

One may think of $c_{j}^{K}u_{j}=s_{i_{j+Kn}}\cdots s_{i_{j+2}}s_{i_{j+1}}u_{j}$ as the location that the billiards trajectory would reach if it were to start at $u_{j}$ and then progress $Kn$ steps, in the absence of any one-way mirrors. Roughly, $\gamma_{j}$ measures the angle between the hyperplane $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}$ and the “limiting direction” of the billiards trajectory.

Note that for all integers $j\geq 0$ and all vectors $\epsilon\in V$ , we have

$$ \pi(c_{j}^{K}\epsilon-\epsilon)=\pi(c_{j}^{K})\pi(\epsilon)-\pi(\epsilon). $$

Since $c_{j}$ is conjugate to $c$ and we have $\pi(c)^{K}=\mathbbm{1}$ , we must also have $\pi(c_{j}^{K})=\mathbbm{1}$ . It follows that $\pi(c_{j}^{K}\epsilon-\epsilon)=0$ , so $c_{j}^{K}\epsilon-\epsilon\in V^{W}$ . Taking $\epsilon=u_{j}\beta$ , we find that $\gamma_{j}\in V^{W}$ for all $j$ . Taking $\epsilon=\alpha_{i_{j}}$ yields that $c_{j}^{K}\alpha_{i_{j}}-\alpha_{i_{j}}\in V^{W}$ for all $j$ .

Next, we will use (19) to relate $\gamma_{j}$ and $\gamma_{j-1}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\gamma_{j} \displaystyle=c_{j}^{K}(s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}\beta+\lambda_{j}\alpha_{i_{j}})-(s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}\beta+\lambda_{j}\alpha_{i_{j}}) \displaystyle=s_{i_{j}}(c_{j-1}^{K}u_{j-1}\beta-u_{j-1}\beta)+\lambda_{j}(c_{j}^{K}\alpha_{i_{j}}-\alpha_{i_{j}}) \displaystyle=s_{i_{j}}\gamma_{j-1}+\lambda_{j}(c_{j}^{K}\alpha_{i_{j}}-\alpha_{i_{j}}) \displaystyle=\gamma_{j-1}+\lambda_{j}(c_{j}^{K}\alpha_{i_{j}}-\alpha_{i_{j}}); $$

in the second equality, we used the fact that $c_{j}s_{i_{j}}=s_{i_{j}}c_{j-1}$ , and in the fourth equality, we used the fact that $\gamma_{j-1}\in V^{W}$ .

By Theorem 5.1, the word $(i_{j+n}\cdots i_{j+1})^{K}i_{j}$ is reduced. Hence, $c_{j}^{K}\alpha_{i_{j}}\in\Phi^{+}$ , and $c_{j}^{K}\alpha_{i_{j}}\neq\alpha_{i_{j}}$ (by (11)). It follows that when $c_{j}^{K}\alpha_{i_{j}}-\alpha_{i_{j}}$ is written in the basis of simple roots, at least one of the coefficients is positive. Since $c_{j}^{K}\alpha_{i_{j}}-\alpha_{i_{j}}\in V^{W}$ , we find that $c_{j}^{K}\alpha_{i_{j}}-\alpha_{i_{j}}$ is a positive real multiple of the imaginary root $\delta$ .

Using (20) together with the fact that $\lambda_{j}\geq 0$ , we find that $\gamma_{j}-\gamma_{j-1}$ is a nonnegative real multiple of $\delta$ for all $j$ . Since the sequence $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ is periodic, it must actually be constant. This implies that $\lambda_{j}=0$ for all $j$ , as desired. ∎

For $\beta\in\Phi$ , let $W^{\beta}$ be the subgroup of $W$ generated by the set

$$ \{r_{\beta^{\prime}}:\text{$\beta^{\prime}\in\Phi$ and $B(\beta,\beta^{\prime})=0$}\}. $$

#### Corollary 5.3.

Let $W$ be an irreducible affine Coxeter group, and let $c$ be a Coxeter element of $W$ . If $c$ is not futuristic, then there exist an integer $K\geq 1$ and a root $\gamma\in\Phi$ such that $c^{K}\in W^{\gamma}$ .

#### Proof.

Let us write $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ , where $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ is a fixed ordering of $I$ . Suppose that $c$ is not futuristic. That is, there exist a nonempty convex set $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ and an element $u_{0}\in W\setminus\mathscr{L}$ such that the corresponding billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ is periodic. By Lemma 3.1, the billiards trajectory is contained in a single proper stratum $\mathrm{Str}(R)$ .

Choose a positive integer $K$ such that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{K}(u_{0})=u_{0}$ and $\pi(c)^{K}=\mathbbm{1}$ . Let $\beta$ be an arbitrary transmitting root of $\mathrm{Str}(R)$ , which exists by Lemma 3.7. We will prove that $c^{K}\in W^{u_{0}\beta}$ . Clearly, $W^{u_{0}\beta}=u_{0}W^{\beta}u_{0}^{-1}$ , so it suffices to prove that

$$ u_{0}^{-1}c^{K}u_{0}\in W^{\beta}. $$

For each $j\geq 1$ , define

$$ t_{j}=u_{j}^{-1}s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}=\begin{cases}r_{u_{j-1}^{-1}\alpha_{i_{j}}}&\mbox{if $u_{j}=u_{j-1}$;}\\
\mathbbm{1}&\mbox{if $u_{j}=s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}$.}\end{cases} $$

In other words, if the billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ hits a one-way mirror at step $j$ , then $t_{j}$ is the reflection corresponding to that one-way mirror; otherwise, $t_{j}$ is the identity. It follows from Theorem 5.2 that $t_{j}\in W^{\beta}$ for all $j\geq 1$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle t_{Kn}t_{Kn-1}\cdots t_{2}t_{1} \displaystyle=(u_{Kn}^{-1}s_{i_{Kn}}u_{Kn-1})(u_{Kn-1}^{-1}s_{i_{Kn-1}}u_{Kn-2})\cdots(u_{2}^{-1}s_{i_{2}}u_{1})(u_{1}^{-1}s_{i_{1}}u_{0}) \displaystyle=u_{Kn}^{-1}(s_{i_{Kn}}\cdots s_{i_{1}})u_{0} \displaystyle=u_{0}^{-1}c^{K}u_{0}, $$

which implies (21). ∎

In the remainder of this section, we address the affine Coxeter groups of types $\widetilde{A}$ , $\widetilde{C}$ , and $\widetilde{G}_{2}$ .

### 5.2. Type $\widetilde{A}$

Fix an integer $n\geq 3$ . An affine permutation of size $n$ is a bijection $u\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ such that $u(j+n)=u(j)+n$ for all $j\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $\sum_{j=1}^{n}u(j)=n(n+1)/2$ . Let $\widetilde{A}_{n-1}$ be the group of affine permutations of size $n$ under composition. For $a,b\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $a\not\equiv b\pmod{n}$ , define

$$ t_{a,b}=\prod_{r\in\mathbb{Z}}(a+rn\,\,\,\,b+rn)\in\widetilde{A}_{n-1}. $$

Note that $t_{a,b}=t_{b,a}=t_{a+kn,b+kn}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Let $s_{i}=t_{i,i+1}$ , and let $S=\{s_{0},\ldots,s_{n-1}\}$ . Then $(\widetilde{A}_{n-1},S)$ is a Coxeter system [2, Section 8.3]. The reflections of $\widetilde{A}_{n-1}$ are precisely the elements $t_{a,b}$ defined in (22). The Coxeter graph of $\widetilde{A}_{n-1}$ is

#### Lemma 5.4.

Let $e_{a}-e_{b}$ and $e_{a^{\prime}}-e_{b^{\prime}}$ be two roots in the root system of type $\widetilde{A}_{n-1}$ . We have ${B(e_{a}-e_{b},e_{a^{\prime}}-e_{b^{\prime}})=0}$ if and only if $a,b,a^{\prime},b^{\prime}$ belong to distinct residue classes modulo $n$ .

#### Proposition 5.5.

For $n\geq 3$ , the Coxeter group $\widetilde{A}_{n-1}$ is futuristic.

#### Proof.

Let us consider acyclic orientations of the $n$ -vertex cycle graph $\Gamma_{\widetilde{A}_{n-1}}$ , as in Section 3.3. For $1\leq d\leq n-1$ , let $c_{(d)}$ be the Coxeter element $s_{d}s_{d+1}\cdots s_{n-1}s_{d-1}s_{d-2}\cdots s_{0}$ . If we draw $\Gamma_{\widetilde{A}_{n-1}}$ in the plane as in (23), then the acyclic orientation $\mathrm{ao}(c_{(d)})$ has exactly $d$ counterclockwise edges. It is a simple exercise to show that two acyclic orientations of $\Gamma_{\widetilde{A}_{n-1}}$ are flip equivalent if and only if they have the same number of edges oriented counterclockwise. It follows that each Coxeter element of $\widetilde{A}_{n-1}$ is conjugate to exactly one of $c_{(1)},c_{(2)},\ldots,c_{(n-1)}$ ; hence, according to Proposition 3.12, we just need to show that each of the $n-1$ Coxeter elements in this list is futuristic. Fix $1\leq d\leq n-1$ , and view $c_{(d)}$ as an affine permutation of size $n$ . By Corollary 5.3, it suffices to prove that $c_{(d)}^{K}\not\in W^{\gamma}$ for every integer $K\geq 1$ and every root $\gamma\in\Phi$ . Fix such $K$ and $\gamma$ , and write $\gamma=e_{a}-e_{b}$ for some integers $a$ and $b$ with $a\not\equiv b\pmod{n}$ . According to Lemma 5.4, the subgroup $W^{\gamma}$ is generated by reflections $t$ that satisfy $t(a)=a$ and $t(b)=b$ . Consequently, we just need to show that $c_{(d)}^{K}(a)\neq a$ .

For $j\in\mathbb{Z}$ , it is straightforward to compute that

$$ c_{(d)}(j)=\begin{cases}j-n+d-1&\mbox{if }j\equiv 1\pmod{n};\\
j-1&\mbox{if }j\equiv 2,3,\ldots,d\pmod{n};\\
j+1&\mbox{if }j\equiv d+1,d+2,\ldots,n-1\pmod{n};\\
n+d+1&\mbox{if }j\equiv n\pmod{n}.\end{cases} $$

From this, one can readily deduce that $c_{(d)}^{K}(j)<j$ if $j\equiv 1,2,\ldots,d\pmod{n}$ and that $c_{(d)}^{K}(j)>j$ if $j\equiv d+1,d+2,\ldots,n\pmod{n}$ . In particular, $c_{(d)}^{K}(a)\neq a$ . ∎

## 6. The Small-Root Billiards Graph

We now proceed to the proofs of Theorems 1.17, 1.18 and 1.16. In each proof, our strategy will be as follows. Let $W$ be a Coxeter group that we wish to prove is futuristic. Let $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ be a nonempty convex set, let $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ be an ordering of $I$ , and let $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ be a corresponding periodic billiards trajectory. Assume for the sake of contradiction that the billiards trajectory is not contained in $\mathscr{L}$ . Then by Lemma 3.1, it is contained within a single proper stratum $\mathrm{Str}(R)$ . By Lemma 3.7, there exists a transmitting root $\beta$ of $\mathrm{Str}(R)$ . By Lemma 3.11, each root $-u_{j}\beta$ is small. Let $\gamma_{j}=-u_{j}\beta$ . The sequence $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ of small roots is highly constrained. First, for each $j\geq 1$ , we have $u_{j}\in\{u_{j-1},s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}\}$ , so $\gamma_{j}\in\{\gamma_{j-1},s_{i_{j}}\gamma_{j-1}\}$ . Moreover, if there exists a positive root $\gamma^{\prime}\neq\gamma_{j-1}$ such that $H^{+}_{\gamma^{\prime}}\cap H^{-}_{\gamma_{j-1}}\cap H^{+}_{\alpha_{i_{j}}}=\varnothing$ , then Lemma 3.8 implies that $u_{j}=s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}$ and (consequently) $\gamma_{j}=s_{i_{j}}\gamma_{j-1}$ .

These considerations show that the distinct $\gamma_{j}$ ’s form a walk on a particular directed graph, which we now define. This graph is similar to the minimal root reflection table of Casselman [5], but it contains some additional information.

#### Definition 6.1.

The small-root billiards graph of $W$ , denoted ${\bf G}_{W}$ , is the following directed graph in which each edge is labeled by an element of $I$ and is either solid or dotted. The vertex set of the small-root billiards graph is $\Sigma\cup\{\ominus\}$ , where $\Sigma$ is the set of small roots and $\ominus$ is a special symbol that represents negative roots. For each $\gamma\in\Sigma$ and $i\in I$ such that $s_{i}\gamma\in\Sigma$ , there is an edge labeled $i$ from $\gamma$ to $s_{i}\gamma$ (this edge is a loop if $s_{i}\gamma=\gamma$ ). The edge from $\gamma$ to $s_{i}\gamma$ is solid if there exists a positive root $\gamma^{\prime}\neq\gamma$ such that $H_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{+}\cap H_{\gamma}^{-}\cap H^{+}_{\alpha_{i}}=\varnothing$ ; otherwise, it is dotted. Additionally, for each $i\in I$ , there is a solid edge labeled $i$ from $\alpha_{i}$ to $\ominus$ . Let $\lambda(e)\in I$ denote the label of an edge $e$ of ${\bf G}_{W}$ .

Figure 7 shows the small-root billiards graph of $\widetilde{G}_{2}$ .

We will always draw the small-root billiards graph with the higher roots nearer the top of the diagram. That is, if $i\in I$ and $\gamma\in\Sigma$ satisfy $s_{i}\gamma=\gamma-2B(\gamma,\alpha_{i})\alpha_{i}\in\Sigma$ , then we will draw the vertex $s_{i}\gamma$ above (respectively, below) the vertex $\gamma$ if $B(\gamma,\alpha_{i})<0$ (respectively, $B(\gamma,\alpha_{i})>0$ ). If $\gamma$ is drawn above $s_{i}\gamma$ , then the edge from $\gamma$ to $s_{i}\gamma$ is solid because we may take $\gamma^{\prime}=s_{i}\gamma$ . Thus, every edge in ${\bf G}_{W}$ that points downward is solid. However, it is also possible for a solid edge to point upward.

The following lemma summarizes the discussion thus far. The fact that the sequence $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ is eventually periodic follows from the fact that $\Sigma$ is finite.

#### Lemma 6.2.

Let $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ be an ordering of $I$ , and let $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ be a corresponding billiards trajectory that is contained in a single proper stratum. Then there is an eventually periodic sequence $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ of small roots such that the following hold for all $j\geq 1$ .

- (i) If $u_{j}=u_{j-1}$ , then $\gamma_{j}=\gamma_{j-1}$ , and there is no solid edge of ${\bf G}_{W}$ labeled $i_{j}$ with source $\gamma_{j-1}$ .

- (ii) If $u_{j}=s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}$ , then there is an edge of ${\bf G}_{W}$ labeled $i_{j}$ from $\gamma_{j-1}$ to $\gamma_{j}$ . (This edge may be either solid or dotted.)

Moreover, if the sequence $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ is periodic, then so is $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ , and the period of $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ divides the period of $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ .

Our next goal is to reformulate Lemma 6.2 in a way that is easier to visualize. The idea of the reformulation is as follows. If $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ is a sequence of roots satisfying the conditions of Lemma 6.2, then we may remove the consecutive duplicates from the sequence $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ to obtain a walk in the graph ${\bf G}_{W}$ . This walk satisfies certain conditions, which we will describe in Definition 6.3 below. First, we must introduce some additional terminology.

Fix an ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ of $I$ . As usual, we may define an infinite periodic sequence $i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},\ldots$ by setting $i_{j+n}=i_{j}$ for all $j\geq 1$ . For any indices $i,i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime}\in I$ , let us say that $i^{\prime}$ is betwixt $i$ and $i^{\prime\prime}$ if for all positive integers $j<j^{\prime\prime}$ with $i_{j}=i$ and $i_{j^{\prime\prime}}=i^{\prime\prime}$ , there exists an integer $j^{\prime}$ with $j<j^{\prime}<j^{\prime\prime}$ and $i_{j^{\prime}}=i^{\prime}$ . Note that this definition is not symmetric in $i$ and $i^{\prime\prime}$ . For $j,j^{\prime},j^{\prime\prime}\in[n]$ , we have that $i_{j^{\prime}}$ is betwixt $i_{j}$ and $i_{j^{\prime\prime}}$ if and only if $j<j^{\prime}<j^{\prime\prime}$ , $j^{\prime}<j^{\prime\prime}\leq j$ , or $j^{\prime\prime}\leq j<j^{\prime}$ .

A closed walk in a directed graph ${G}$ is a pair $\mathcal{C}=((v_{1},\ldots,v_{d}),(e_{1},\ldots,e_{d}))$ , where $d>0$ is an integer, $v_{1},\ldots,v_{d}$ are vertices of ${G}$ , and for each $j\in[d]$ , $e_{j}$ is an edge of ${G}$ from $v_{j}$ to $v_{j+1}$ ; here we use the convention $v_{d+1}=v_{1}$ .

#### Definition 6.3.

Let $\mathcal{C}=((v_{1},\ldots,v_{d}),(e_{1},\ldots,e_{d}))$ be a closed walk in the small-root billiards graph ${\bf G}_{W}$ . We say that $\mathcal{C}$ is billiards-plausible (with respect to the ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ of $I$ ) if it satisfies the following two properties.

- (i) For each $j\in[d]$ , there is no solid edge with source $v_{j}$ whose label is betwixt $\lambda(e_{j-1})$ and $\lambda(e_{j})$ . Here, we use the convention $e_{0}=e_{d}$ .

- (ii) We have $s_{\lambda(e_{1})}\cdots s_{\lambda(e_{d})}=\mathbbm{1}$ .

#### Lemma 6.4.

If there does not exist a closed walk in ${\bf G}_{W}$ that is billiards-plausible with respect to the ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ , then the Coxeter element $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ is futuristic.

#### Proof.

We prove the contrapositive. Assume that $c$ is not futuristic. Then there exist a nonempty convex subset $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ and a periodic billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ that is not contained in $\mathscr{L}$ . Let $K>0$ be an integer such that $u_{0}=u_{Kn}$ .

Let $j_{1},\ldots,j_{d}$ be the elements of the set $\{j\in[Kn]:u_{j}=s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}\}$ in increasing order. We have

$$ \mathbbm{1}=u_{0}u_{Kn}^{-1}=(u_{0}u_{1}^{-1})(u_{1}u_{2}^{-1})\cdots(u_{Kn-2}u_{Kn-1}^{-1})(u_{Kn-1}u_{Kn}^{-1}). $$

For each $j\in[Kn]$ , the factor $u_{j-1}u_{j}^{-1}$ equals $\mathbbm{1}$ if $u_{j}=u_{j-1}$ and equals $s_{i_{j}}$ if $u_{j}=s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}$ . Removing the identity terms from the product in (24) thus yields

$$ s_{i_{j_{1}}}\cdots s_{i_{j_{d}}}=\mathbbm{1}. $$

Now, let $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ be the sequence from Lemma 6.2. For each $k\in[d]$ , let $e_{k}$ be the edge of ${\bf G}_{W}$ labeled $i_{j_{k}}$ from $\gamma_{j_{k}-1}$ to $\gamma_{j_{k}}$ . By Lemma 6.2(i), the edges $e_{1},\ldots,e_{d}$ form a closed walk $\mathcal{C}$ satisfying Definition 6.3(i). It follows from (25) that $\mathcal{C}$ also satisfies Definition 6.3(ii), so $\mathcal{C}$ is billiards-plausible. ∎

For an example of how Lemma 6.4 can be used to prove that several Coxeter groups are futuristic, see the proof of Theorem 1.18 in Section 9.

The proof of Lemma 6.4 gives a procedure for constructing a billiards-plausible closed walk $\mathcal{C}$ from a periodic billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ in a proper stratum. We say that the trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ is a lift of $\mathcal{C}$ .

It is natural to ask if the converse of Lemma 6.4 holds.

#### Question 6.5.

Suppose ${\bf G}_{W}$ has a closed walk that is billiards-plausible with respect to the ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ . Is the Coxeter element $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ necessarily not futuristic?

#### Lemma 6.6.

If there does not exist a closed walk in ${\bf G}_{W}$ that satisfies Definition 6.3(i) with respect to the ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ , then the Coxeter element $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ is superfuturistic.

#### Proof.

We prove the contrapositive. Assume that $c$ is not superfuturistic. Then there exist a nonempty convex subset $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ and a billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ that does not eventually reach $\mathscr{L}$ . By Lemma 3.1, we have

$$ \mathrm{Sep}(u_{0})\supseteq\mathrm{Sep}(u_{1})\supseteq\mathrm{Sep}(u_{2})\supseteq\cdots. $$

By Lemma 3.3, the sequence $\mathrm{Sep}(u_{0}),\mathrm{Sep}(u_{1}),\mathrm{Sep}(u_{2}),\ldots$ is eventually constant. We may assume that this sequence is constant and the billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ is contained within a single stratum $\mathrm{Str}(R)$ .

Let $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ be the sequence from Lemma 6.2, and let $K>0$ be an integer such that $Kn$ is divisible by the period of the sequence $\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots$ . As in the proof of Lemma 6.4, let $j_{1},\ldots,j_{d}$ be the elements of the set $\{j\in[Kn]:u_{j}=s_{i_{j}}u_{j-1}\}$ in increasing order. For each $k\in[d]$ , let $e_{k}$ be the edge of ${\bf G}_{W}$ labeled $j_{k}$ from $\gamma_{j_{k}-1}$ to $\gamma_{j_{k}}$ . By Lemma 6.2(i), the edges $e_{1},\ldots,e_{d}$ form a closed walk $\mathcal{C}$ satisfying Definition 6.3(i). ∎

We now prove some lemmas that will help us determine whether the edges of $\mathbf{G}_{W}$ are solid or dotted.

#### Lemma 6.7.

Let $\gamma\in\Sigma$ and $i\in I$ . Suppose that when $\gamma$ is written in the basis of the simple roots, the coefficient of $\alpha_{i}$ is zero. If there is an edge labeled $i$ from $\gamma$ to $s_{i}\gamma$ in $\mathbf{G}_{W}$ , then it is dotted.

#### Proof.

Assume for the sake of contradiction that there is a solid edge from $\gamma$ to $s_{i}\gamma$ . Then there is a root $\gamma^{\prime}\in\Phi^{+}\setminus\{\gamma\}$ such that $H_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{+}\cap H_{\gamma}^{-}\cap H_{\alpha_{i}}^{+}=\varnothing$ .

Let $t=r_{\gamma}$ and $t^{\prime}=r_{\gamma^{\prime}}$ be the reflections corresponding to $\gamma$ and $\gamma^{\prime}$ , respectively. We have $t\in H_{\gamma}^{-}$ . Also, $t$ lies in the parabolic subgroup $W_{I\setminus\{i\}}$ . In particular, $t$ does not have $s_{i}$ as a right inversion, so $t\in H_{\alpha_{i}}^{+}$ . Since $H_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{+}\cap H_{\gamma}^{-}\cap H_{\alpha_{i}}^{+}=\varnothing$ , we have $t\not\in H_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{+}$ . Hence, $t$ must have $t^{\prime}$ as a right inversion. It follows that $t^{\prime}$ also lies in the parabolic subgroup $W_{I\setminus\{i\}}$ , so $\gamma^{\prime}$ is a root of $W_{I\setminus\{i\}}$ .

The fact that $H_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{+}\cap H_{\gamma}^{-}\cap H_{\alpha_{i}}^{+}=\varnothing$ tells us that $H_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{+}\cap H_{\alpha_{i}}^{+}\subseteq H_{\gamma}^{+}$ . Because $W_{I\setminus\{i\}}\subseteq H_{\alpha_{i}}^{+}$ , we have

$$ H_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{+}\cap W_{I\setminus\{i\}}\subseteq H_{\gamma}^{+}\cap W_{I\setminus\{i\}}. $$

But $H_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{+}\cap W_{I\setminus\{i\}}$ and $H_{\gamma}^{+}\cap W_{I\setminus\{i\}}$ are the half-spaces of $W_{I\setminus\{i\}}$ corresponding to $\gamma^{\prime}$ and $\gamma$ , respectively. Hence, $\gamma$ is not a small root of $W_{I\setminus\{i\}}$ . This contradicts Corollary 2.5. ∎

#### Lemma 6.8.

Let $\gamma\in\Sigma$ and $i\in I$ . Suppose that there exist real numbers $a,a^{\prime}>0$ such that $a\gamma-a^{\prime}\alpha_{i}\in\Phi$ . If there is an edge from $\gamma$ to $s_{i}\gamma$ in $\mathbf{G}_{W}$ , then it is solid.

#### Proof.

Let $\gamma^{\prime}=a\gamma-a^{\prime}\alpha_{i}$ . Then $H_{\gamma^{\prime}}^{+}\cap H_{\gamma}^{-}\cap H_{\alpha_{i}}^{+}=\varnothing$ , so the edge from $\gamma$ to $s_{i}\gamma$ is solid. ∎

### 6.1. Small Roots of Rank-2 Parabolic Subgroups

The proofs of Theorems 1.16, 1.17 and 1.18 will involve explicitly computing ${\bf G}_{W}$ for various Coxeter groups $W$ and applying Lemma 6.2 or Lemma 6.4. In this subsection, we will show that ${\bf G}_{W}$ always has a certain easily described induced subgraph.

Let $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ be distinct indices such that $m(i,i^{\prime})<\infty$ , and let $m=m(i,i^{\prime})$ . It follows from a routine computation that the roots of the standard rank- $2$ parabolic subgroup $W_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}$ are the vectors

$$ \alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)=\frac{\sin((k+1)\pi/m)}{\sin(\pi/m)}\alpha_{i}+\frac{\sin(k\pi/m)}{\sin(\pi/m)}\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\in V, $$

where $k$ ranges over the integers. The vector $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)$ depends only on the residue class of $k$ modulo $2m$ , and distinct residue classes yield distinct vectors $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)$ , so the number of roots of $W_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}$ is $2m$ . Geometrically, the restriction of $B$ to the $2$ -dimensional space $V_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\}\subseteq V$ is a real inner product, and $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(0),\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(1),\ldots,\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(2m-1)$ are $2m$ equally spaced vectors (in that order) on the unit circle of $V_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}$ . The simple roots of $W_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}$ are $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(0)=\alpha_{i}$ and $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m-1)=\alpha_{i^{\prime}}$ . The action of $W_{\{i,i^{\prime}\}}$ on the roots is given by $s_{i}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m-k)$ and $s_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m-2-k)$ .

Let $\Sigma_{\leq 2}$ denote the set

$$ \{\alpha_{i}:i\in I\}\cup\{\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k):\text{$i,i^{\prime}\in I$ are distinct},\,\,m(i,i^{\prime})<\infty,\,\,0<k<m(i,i^{\prime})-1\}. $$

Note that since $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)=\alpha_{i^{\prime},i}(m(i,i^{\prime})-1-k)$ , we have listed each element of $\Sigma_{\leq 2}\setminus\{\alpha_{i}:i\in I\}$ twice in (26). Let ${\bf G}_{W,\leq 2}$ denote the induced subgraph of ${\bf G}_{W}$ on the vertex set $\Sigma_{\leq 2}\cup\{\ominus\}$ .

#### Lemma 6.9.

The set $\Sigma_{\leq 2}$ consists of all small roots that can be written as linear combinations of at most two simple roots. Moreover, the edges of ${\bf G}_{W,\leq 2}$ are as follows.

- (i) For each pair $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ of distinct indices with $m(i,i^{\prime})<\infty$ and for each integer $k$ satisfying $0<k<m(i,i^{\prime})-1$ , there is a solid edge labeled $i$ from $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)$ to $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m(i,i^{\prime})-k)$ .

- (ii) For each pair $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ of distinct indices with $m(i,i^{\prime})<\infty$ , there is a dotted edge labeled $i$ from $\alpha_{i^{\prime}}$ to $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(1)$ . (If $m(i,i^{\prime})=2$ , then this edge is a loop.)

- (iii) For each triple $i,i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime}\in I$ of distinct indices with $2=m(i,i^{\prime})=m(i,i^{\prime\prime})<m(i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime})<\infty$ and for each integer $k$ satisfying $0<k<m(i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime})-1$ , there is a dotted edge labeled $i$ from $\alpha_{i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime}}(k)$ to itself.

- (iv) For each $i\in I$ , there is a solid edge labeled $i$ from $\alpha_{i}$ to $\ominus$ .

#### Proof.

The first statement in the lemma follows from Corollary 2.5.

Let $\gamma\in\Sigma_{\leq 2}$ and $i\in I$ . Upon inspection, we find that $s_{i}\gamma\in\Sigma_{\leq 2}$ if and only if one of the following conditions holds:

- (i) We have $\gamma=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)$ , where $i^{\prime}\in I$ satisfies $m(i,i^{\prime})<\infty$ and $k$ is an integer such that $0<k<m(i,i^{\prime})-1$ . In this case, $s_{i}\gamma=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m(i,i^{\prime})-k)$ .

- (ii) We have $\gamma=\alpha_{i^{\prime}}$ , where $i^{\prime}\in I$ satisfies $m(i,i^{\prime})<\infty$ . In this case, $s_{i}\gamma=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(1)$ .

- (iii) We have $\gamma=\alpha_{i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime}}(k)$ , where $i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime}\in I$ satisfy $2=m(i,i^{\prime})=m(i,i^{\prime\prime})<m(i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime})<\infty$ and $k$ is an integer such that $0<k<m(i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime})-1$ . In this case, $s_{i}\gamma=\gamma$ .

Together with the edge from $\alpha_{i}$ to $\ominus$ for each $i$ , this completes the description of the set of edges of ${\bf G}_{W,\leq 2}$ . We use Lemmas 6.7 and 6.8 to determine which edges are solid and which edges are dotted. ∎

Let us use Lemma 6.9 to briefly discuss the graph structure of ${\bf G}_{W,\leq 2}$ , ignoring for now whether edges are solid or dotted. As mentioned above, $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)=\alpha_{i^{\prime},i}(m(i,i^{\prime})-1-k)$ . Let $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ be distinct indices. If $m=m(i,i^{\prime})$ is an odd integer, then ${\bf G}_{W,\leq 2}$ has a bidirectional path

$$ \alpha_{i}=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(0)\underset{i^{\prime}}{\longleftrightarrow}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m-2)\underset{i}{\longleftrightarrow}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(2)\underset{i^{\prime}}{\longleftrightarrow}\cdots\underset{i^{\prime}}{\longleftrightarrow}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(1)\underset{i}{\longleftrightarrow}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m-1)=\alpha_{i^{\prime}} $$

with $m$ vertices and $m-1$ edges in each direction. If instead $m=m(i,i^{\prime})$ is an even integer, then we obtain the two disjoint bidirectional paths

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{i} \displaystyle=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(0)\underset{i^{\prime}}{\longleftrightarrow}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m-2)\underset{i}{\longleftrightarrow}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(2)\underset{i^{\prime}}{\longleftrightarrow}\cdots\longleftrightarrow\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(2\lfloor m/4\rfloor)\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\alpha_{i^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m-1)\underset{i}{\longleftrightarrow}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(1)\underset{i^{\prime}}{\longleftrightarrow}\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(m-3)\underset{i}{\longleftrightarrow}\cdots\longleftrightarrow\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(2\lfloor(m-2)/4\rfloor+1), $$

each of which has $m/2$ vertices and $m/2-1$ edges in each direction; there are also loops at the vertices $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(2\lfloor m/4\rfloor)$ and $\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(2\lfloor(m-2)/4\rfloor+1)$ . (The labels of these loops and of the rightmost edges in these bidirectional paths depend on the parity of $m/2$ .) Regardless of the parity of $m$ , each vertex in one of these paths also has a loop labeled $i^{\prime\prime}$ for each index $i^{\prime\prime}\in I$ such that ${m(i,i^{\prime\prime})=m(i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime})=2}$ .

## 7. Right-Angled Coxeter Groups

The Coxeter group $W$ is called right-angled if $m(i,i^{\prime})\in\{2,\infty\}$ for all distinct $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ . We now prove Theorem 1.16, which states that every right-angled Coxeter group is superfuturistic.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.16.

Let $W$ be a right-angled Coxeter group. By Proposition 2.4, the set $\Sigma$ of small roots of $W$ is equal to the set $\{\alpha_{i}:i\in I\}$ of simple roots. In the small-root billiards graph ${\bf G}_{W}$ , there is a dotted edge labeled $i$ from $\alpha_{i^{\prime}}$ to itself for all $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ with $m(i,i^{\prime})=2$ . There is also a solid edge labeled $i$ from $\alpha_{i}$ to $\ominus$ for all $i\in I$ . There are no other edges. See Figure 8 for an example.

## 8. Coxeter Groups with Complete Coxeter Graphs

Theorem 1.17 states that if the Coxeter graph of a Coxeter group $W$ is complete, then $W$ is futuristic. To prove this, we will show that the small-root billiards graph ${\bf G}_{W}$ is actually equal to the graph ${\bf G}_{W,\leq 2}$ that we described in Lemma 6.9 and the subsequent paragraphs. See Figure 9 for an example.

#### Lemma 8.1.

If the Coxeter graph of $W$ is complete, then $\Sigma_{\leq 2}=\Sigma$ .

#### Proof.

By Proposition 2.4, it suffices to prove that for all $i\in I$ and all $\gamma\in\Sigma_{\leq 2}\setminus\{\alpha_{i}\}$ , we have either $s_{i}\gamma\in\Sigma_{\leq 2}$ or $B(\gamma,\alpha_{i})\leq-1$ . For this, there are two inequalities to check. First, we must show that for all $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ with $m(i,i^{\prime})=\infty$ , we have $B(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i^{\prime}})\leq-1$ . Second, we must show that for all distinct $i,i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime}\in I$ with $m(i,i^{\prime})<\infty$ and for all $k$ with $0<k<m(i,i^{\prime})-1$ , we have $B(\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k),\alpha_{i^{\prime\prime}})\leq-1$ . The first inequality follows from the definition of the bilinear form $B$ . For the second, we have

$$ \displaystyle B(\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k),\alpha_{i^{\prime\prime}}) \displaystyle=-\frac{\sin((k+1)\pi/m(i,i^{\prime}))}{\sin(\pi/m(i,i^{\prime}))}\cos(\pi/m(i,i^{\prime\prime}))-\frac{\sin(k\pi/m(i,i^{\prime}))}{\sin(\pi/m(i,i^{\prime}))}\cos(\pi/m(i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime})) \displaystyle\leq-\cos(\pi/m(i,i^{\prime\prime}))-\cos(\pi/m(i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime})) \displaystyle\leq-1, $$

where we have used the inequalities $0<k<m(i,i^{\prime})-1$ and $m(i,i^{\prime\prime}),m(i^{\prime},i^{\prime\prime})\geq 3$ . ∎

To prove Theorem 1.17, all that remains is to carefully apply Lemma 6.4.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.17.

Let $W$ be a Coxeter group with a complete Coxeter graph. Let $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ be an ordering of $I$ , and assume for the sake of contradiction that $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ is not futuristic. By Lemma 6.4, there is a billiards-plausible closed walk $\mathcal{C}=((v_{1},\ldots,v_{d}),(e_{1},\ldots,e_{d}))$ in ${\bf G}_{W}$ .

By Definition 6.3(ii), we have $s_{\lambda(e_{1})}\cdots s_{\lambda(e_{d})}=\mathbbm{1}$ . Therefore, by Matsumoto’s theorem (Theorem 2.1), it is possible to apply a nil move or a braid move to the word $\lambda(e_{1})\cdots\lambda(e_{d})$ .

Suppose first that it is possible to apply a nil move to the word $\lambda(e_{1})\cdots\lambda(e_{d})$ . Then there are two consecutive edges $e_{j-1},e_{j}$ of the walk $\mathcal{C}$ such that $\lambda(e_{j-1})=\lambda(e_{j})$ . Every element of $I\setminus\{\lambda(e_{j})\}$ is betwixt $\lambda(e_{j-1})$ and $\lambda(e_{j})$ . Therefore, by Definition 6.3(i), there are no solid edges in ${\bf G}_{W}$ with source $v_{j}$ , except possibly $e_{j}$ .

By Lemma 8.1, either $v_{j}=\alpha_{i}$ for some $i\in I$ , or $v_{j}=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)$ , where $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ satisfy $m(i,i^{\prime})<\infty$ and $k$ is an integer such that $0<k<m(i,i^{\prime})-1$ . If $v_{j}=\alpha_{i}$ for some $i\in I$ , then there is a solid edge from $v_{j}$ to $\ominus$ . If instead $v_{j}=\alpha_{i,i^{\prime}}(k)$ , then by Lemma 6.9, there are two solid edges with source $v_{j}$ : one labeled $i$ and one labeled $i^{\prime}$ . In either case, we obtain a contradiction with the fact that $e_{j}$ is the only possible solid edge in ${\bf G}_{W}$ with source $v_{j}$ .

Now suppose that it is possible to apply a braid move to the word $\lambda(e_{1})\cdots\lambda(e_{d})$ . Then there exist indices $i,i^{\prime}\in I$ such that the closed walk $\mathcal{C}$ has $m(i,i^{\prime})$ consecutive edges whose labels alternate between $i$ and $i^{\prime}$ . However, by Lemmas 6.9 and 8.1, any walk in ${\bf G}_{W}$ that does not use the vertex $\ominus$ and whose edge labels alternate between $i$ and $i^{\prime}$ must have at most $m(i,i^{\prime})-1$ edges. Again, we obtain a contradiction. ∎

## 9. Coxeter Groups of Rank at Most 3

We now have all the tools we need to prove Theorem 1.18, which states that all Coxeter groups of rank at most 3 are futuristic.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.18.

All Coxeter groups of rank at most 2 are futuristic by Theorems 1.14 and 1.16. Let $W$ be a Coxeter group of rank $3$ . We wish to show that $W$ is futuristic. Without loss of generality, we may assume that the index set $I$ is $\{1,2,3\}$ . Let $p=m(1,3)$ , $q=m(1,2)$ , and $r=m(2,3)$ , and assume without loss of generality that $p\leq q\leq r$ . We now consider several cases depending on the values of $p$ , $q$ , and $r$ .

Case 1. ( $p=q=2$ )

In this case, $W$ is reducible, and its irreducible factors are futuristic because they each have rank at most $2$ . Therefore, $W$ is futuristic (see Remark 2.2).

Case 2. ( $p=2$ , $q=3$ , and $r\leq 5$ )

In this case, it follows from the classification of finite Coxeter groups [2, Appendix A1] that $W$ is finite, so it is futuristic by Theorem 1.14.

Case 3. ( $p=2$ , $q=3$ , and $r=6$ )

In this case, $W$ is the affine Coxeter group $\widetilde{G}_{2}$ . The small-root billiards graph ${\mathbf{G}}_{W}$ is depicted in Figure 7. By Lemma 6.4, $s_{3}s_{2}s_{1}$ is futuristic. By Corollary 3.13, $W$ is futuristic.

Case 4. ( $p=2$ , $q=3$ , and $7\leq r<\infty$ )

## 10. Ancient Coxeter Groups

We now shift gears and construct examples of ancient Coxeter groups.

Let us outline the strategy that led us to the arguments presented below. The Coxeter graph of each Coxeter group $W$ considered in this section is a tree, so in order to prove that $W$ is ancient, it suffices (by Corollary 3.13) to prove that a single fixed Coxeter element of $W$ is not futuristic. To do so, we first construct a candidate periodic sequence $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ . Next, we attempt to find a nonempty convex subset $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ , not containing $u_{0}$ , such that $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ is a periodic billiards trajectory with respect to $\mathscr{L}$ . The machinery of Section 6 tells us that we should take $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ to be a lift of a billiards-plausible closed walk in the corresponding small-root billiards graph.

It will be helpful to keep in mind an alternative definition of noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles that uses reflections rather than roots. Let $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ be a nonempty convex set, and let $i\in I$ and $u\in W$ . Then $\tau_{i}(u)=u$ if either every element of $\mathscr{L}\cup\{u\}$ has $u^{-1}s_{i}u$ as a right inversion or no element of $\mathscr{L}\cup\{u\}$ has $u^{-1}s_{i}u$ as a right inversion. Otherwise, $\tau_{i}(u)=s_{i}u$ . For each reflection $t$ , the hyperplane $\mathrm{H}_{\beta_{t}}$ is a one-way mirror if and only if either every element of $\mathscr{L}$ has $t$ as a right inversion or no element of $\mathscr{L}$ has $t$ as a right inversion.

If $J\subseteq I$ is such that the standard parabolic subgroup $W_{J}$ is finite, then we write $w_{\circ}(J)$ for the long element of $W_{J}$ .

## 11. Classical Billiards (Light Beams)

We now briefly discuss how our Bender–Knuth billiards systems relate to more classical billiards systems studied in dynamics (as in [16, 20, 25, 34]).

As before, let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system whose simple reflections are indexed by a finite set $I$ ; we will assume that $|I|\geq 2$ . Recall that $\mathbb{B}W$ is the Tits cone of $W$ . A ray is a continuous function $\mathfrak{r}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{B}W$ such that $\mathfrak{r}(t)\neq 0$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ , the positive projectivization $\overline{\mathfrak{r}}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B}W)$ is locally injective, and the image of $\mathfrak{r}$ is contained in a 2-dimensional subspace of $V^{*}$ .

#### Example 11.1.

If $W$ is finite, then $\mathbb{B}W=V^{*}$ . In this case, for any two linearly independent vectors $\gamma,\gamma^{\prime}\in V^{*}$ , there is a ray $\mathfrak{r}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{B}W$ defined by

$$ \mathfrak{r}(t)=\cos(t)\gamma+\sin(t)\gamma^{\prime}. $$

#### Definition 11.2.

Let us say that a continuous, piecewise linear curve $\mathfrak{q}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{B}W$ is cordial if it satisfies the following conditions:

- (i) There are infinitely many real numbers $t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ such that $\mathfrak{q}(t)\in\bigcup_{\mathrm{H}\in\mathcal{H}_{W}}\mathrm{H}$ .

- (ii) For any fixed real number $b$ , there are only finitely many real numbers $t$ with $0\leq t\leq b$ such that $\mathfrak{q}(t)\in\bigcup_{\mathrm{H}\in\mathcal{H}_{W}}\mathrm{H}$ .

- (iii) For all $\beta,\beta^{\prime}\in\Phi$ such that $B(\beta,\beta^{\prime})\neq 0$ , the image of $\mathfrak{q}$ does not intersect $\mathrm{H}_{\beta}\cap\mathrm{H}_{\beta^{\prime}}$ .

Let $\mathfrak{r}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{B}W$ be a cordial ray such that $\mathfrak{r}(0)\not\in\bigcup_{\mathrm{H}\in\mathcal{H}_{W}}\mathrm{H}$ . Consider the open regions of the Coxeter arrangement through which the curve $\mathfrak{r}$ passes. We obtain a sequence $v_{0},v_{1},v_{2},\ldots$ of elements of $W$ and a sequence $0=t_{0}<t_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots$ of real numbers with the property that for all nonnegative integers $k$ and all real numbers $t$ with $t_{k}<t<t_{k+1}$ , we have $\mathfrak{q}(t)\in\mathbb{B}^{\circ}v_{k}$ , where $\mathbb{B}^{\circ}$ denotes the interior of $\mathbb{B}$ . Although $\mathfrak{r}$ is a continuous curve, the regions $\mathbb{B}v_{k-1}$ and $\mathbb{B}v_{k}$ can be nonadjacent in the Coxeter arrangement since $\mathfrak{r}(t_{k})$ can lie on multiple hyperplanes of $\mathcal{H}_{W}$ . Put differently, it is possible that $v_{k}v_{k-1}^{-1}$ is not a simple reflection. However, (iii) guarantees that for each integer $k\geq 1$ , the hyperplanes in $\mathcal{H}_{W}$ that contain $\mathfrak{r}(t_{k})$ are pairwise orthogonal. Since $\mathfrak{q}(t_{k})$ lies in both $\mathbb{B}v_{k-1}$ and $\mathbb{B}v_{k}$ , we conclude that $v_{k}v_{k-1}^{-1}$ is a product of distinct simple reflections that commute pairwise. Let $J_{k}(\mathfrak{r})$ denote the set of the indices of these simple reflections. Then $J_{k}(\mathfrak{r})$ is an independent set (i.e., a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices) of the Coxeter graph $\Gamma_{W}$ .

#### Definition 11.3.

Let $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ be an ordering of the elements of $I$ , and let $i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},\ldots$ be the infinite sequence satisfying $i_{j+n}=i_{j}$ for every positive integer $j$ . We say that the ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ is luminous if there exists a cordial ray $\mathfrak{r}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{B}W$ such that the sequence $i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},\ldots$ consists of the elements of $J_{1}(\mathfrak{r})$ in some order, followed by the elements of $J_{2}(\mathfrak{r})$ in some order, followed by the elements of $J_{3}(\mathfrak{r})$ in some order, and so on. In this case, we say that $\mathfrak{r}$ certifies that $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ is luminous.

Let $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ be a luminous ordering of the elements of $I$ , and let $i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},\ldots$ be the infinite sequence satisfying $i_{j+n}=i_{j}$ for every positive integer $j$ . Let $\mathfrak{r}$ be a cordial ray that certifies that $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ is luminous, and let $J_{k}=J_{k}(\mathfrak{r})$ . That is, for every $k\geq 1$ , we have

$$ J_{k}=\{i_{j+1},\ldots,i_{j+|J_{k}|}\}, $$

where $j=|J_{1}|+\cdots+|J_{k-1}|$ . Let $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ be a convex set, and let $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ be a billiards trajectory defined with respect to the ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ . We will now describe how to “fold” the ray $\mathfrak{r}$ into a cordial curve $\mathfrak{p}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{B}W$ , which we call a light beam. The light beam $\mathfrak{p}$ will reflect off of the one-way mirrors of the convex set $\mathscr{L}$ as in classical billiards, and we can think of the Bender–Knuth billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ as a discretization of $\mathfrak{p}$ .

For each independent set $J=\{j_{1},\ldots,j_{d}\}\subseteq I$ of the Coxeter graph $\Gamma_{W}$ , define

$$ s_{J}=s_{j_{1}}\cdots s_{j_{d}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tau_{J}=\tau_{j_{1}}\cdots\tau_{j_{d}}; $$

since $J$ is independent, the order of the multiplication used to define $s_{J}$ does not matter, nor does the order of the composition used to define $\tau_{J}$ .

After multiplying $\mathfrak{r}$ on the right by a suitable element of $W$ , we may assume that $\mathfrak{r}(0)$ lies in the region $\mathbb{B}^{\circ}u_{0}$ . Recall that there exist a sequence $v_{0},v_{1},v_{2},\ldots$ of elements of $W$ and a sequence $0=t_{0}<t_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots$ of positive real numbers such that $\mathfrak{q}(t)\in\mathbb{B}^{\circ}v_{k}$ for all nonnegative integers $k$ and all real numbers $t$ with $t_{k}<t<t_{k+1}$ . We have

$$ v_{k}=s_{J_{k}}s_{J_{k-1}}\cdots s_{J_{1}}u_{0}. $$

Therefore, the ray $\mathfrak{r}$ passes consecutively through the open regions

$$ \mathbb{B}^{\circ}u_{0},\,\mathbb{B}^{\circ}s_{J_{1}}u_{0},\,\mathbb{B}^{\circ}s_{J_{2}}s_{J_{1}}u_{0},\,\mathbb{B}^{\circ}s_{J_{3}}s_{J_{2}}s_{J_{1}}u_{0},\ldots $$

of the Coxeter arrangement. The light beam $\mathfrak{p}$ will be constructed so that it instead passes consecutively through the open regions

$$ \mathbb{B}^{\circ}u_{0},\,\mathbb{B}^{\circ}\tau_{J_{1}}(u_{0}),\,\mathbb{B}^{\circ}\tau_{J_{2}}\tau_{J_{1}}(u_{0}),\,\mathbb{B}^{\circ}\tau_{J_{3}}\tau_{J_{2}}\tau_{J_{1}}(u_{0}),\ldots. $$

Note that the elements $u_{0},\tau_{J_{1}}(u_{0}),\tau_{J_{2}}\tau_{J_{1}}(u_{0}),\tau_{J_{3}}\tau_{J_{2}}\tau_{J_{1}}(u_{0}),\ldots$ form a subsequence of the billiards trajectory $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ .

Define the function $\mathfrak{p}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{B}W$ via

$$ \mathfrak{p}(t)=\mathfrak{r}(t)(s_{J_{k}}\cdots s_{J_{1}}u_{0})^{-1}(\tau_{J_{k}}\cdots\tau_{J_{1}}(u_{0})) $$

for all integers $k\geq 0$ and all real numbers $t$ with $t_{k}\leq t<t_{k+1}$ . It is not difficult to check that $\mathfrak{p}$ is a continuous, piecewise linear, and cordial curve. The positive projectivization $\overline{\mathfrak{p}}\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B}W)$ is a curve that travels along a linear path unless it hits the reflective side of a one-way mirror of $\mathscr{L}$ , at which point it reflects off of that one-way mirror. It is possible to equip $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B}W)$ with a metric [25, Section 2] in such a way that when the light beam $\overline{\mathfrak{p}}$ reflects off of a one-way mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. With this metric, $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B}W)$ is isometric to a sphere if $W$ is finite, to a Euclidean space if $W$ is affine, and to a hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^{n-1}$ if $W$ is hyperbolic (i.e., if the bilinear form $B\colon V\times V\to\mathbb{R}$ has signature $(n-1,1)$ , where $n=|I|$ is the rank of $W$ ). For examples of light beams reflecting in this manner, see the thin cyan curves in Figures 1 and 4.77 7 When the thin cyan curve in Figure 2 reflects off the hyperplane $\mathrm{H}_{e_{1}-e_{3}}$ , the angle of incidence does not appear to be equal to the angle of reflection. This is because Figure 2 is drawn not-to-scale and angles are distorted.

Let us highlight two settings where it is known that an ordering is luminous. Both of these settings are discussed in [25].

The first setting is that in which $\Gamma_{W}$ is bipartite. Let $I=Q\sqcup Q^{\prime}$ be a bipartition of $\Gamma_{W}$ ; we may assume that $Q$ and $Q^{\prime}$ are both nonempty. Let $i_{1},\ldots,i_{q}$ be an ordering of $Q$ , and let $i_{q+1},\ldots,i_{n}$ be an ordering of $Q^{\prime}$ . The base region $\mathbb{B}$ is a cone whose facets correspond to the elements of $I$ . For $i\in I$ , let $F_{i}$ be the facet of $\mathbb{B}$ that separates $\mathbb{B}$ from $\mathbb{B}s_{i}$ . Let $\mathcal{F}_{Q}=\bigcap_{i\in Q}F_{i}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{Q^{\prime}}=\bigcap_{i\in Q^{\prime}}F_{i}$ . We can choose $z\in\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{F}_{Q})$ and $z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{F}_{Q^{\prime}})$ so that the line $\mathfrak{l}$ passing through $z$ and $z^{\prime}$ is orthogonal to both $\mathcal{F}_{Q}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{Q^{\prime}}$ (here, orthogonality is defined with respect to the Hilbert metric on $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B}W)$ , as defined in [25]). Let $x_{0}$ be a point on the line $\mathfrak{l}$ that lies in the interior of $\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{B})$ . ## 12. Futuristic Directions

### 12.1. Characterizations

The most outstanding open problem arising from this paper is that of characterizing futuristic Coxeter groups and ancient Coxeter groups. Let us mention some smaller questions that might be more tractable.

Say a Coxeter group $W$ is contemporary if it is neither futuristic nor ancient. In other words, $W$ is contemporary if there exist Coxeter elements $c$ and $c^{\prime}$ of $W$ such that $c$ is futuristic while $c^{\prime}$ is not.

#### Question 12.1.

Do contemporary Coxeter groups exist?

Note that Corollary 3.13 tells us that a Coxeter group whose Coxeter graph is a forest cannot be contemporary.

Every minimally non-futuristic Coxeter group that we have found is also minimally ancient. Moreover, every minimally ancient Coxeter group that we have found has only finite edge labels in its Coxeter graph. This leads us naturally to the following questions.

#### Question 12.2.

Does there exist a minimally ancient Coxeter group $W$ such that at least one edge of $\Gamma_{W}$ is labeled $\infty$ ?

#### Question 12.3.

Does there exist a minimally non-futuristic Coxeter group $W$ such that at least one edge of $\Gamma_{W}$ is labeled $\infty$ ?

### 12.2. Periodic Points

Let $c$ be a Coxeter element of $W$ , and let $\mathscr{L}\subseteq W$ be a convex set that is not heavy with respect to $c$ . By definition, $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}$ has a periodic point outside of $\mathscr{L}$ . It would be interesting to gain a better understanding of these periodic points.

### 12.3. Billiards-Plausible Closed Walks

In Question 6.5, we asked whether the converse to Lemma 6.4 holds. In other words, if there exists a closed walk in ${\bf G}_{W}$ that is billiards-plausible with respect to an ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ of $I$ , does it follow that the Coxeter element $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ is not futuristic? (The stronger statement that every billiards-plausible closed walk in ${\bf G}_{W}$ lifts to a billiards trajectory is false; there is a counterexample with $W=\widetilde{E}_{8}$ .)

### 12.4. Decidability

Is there an algorithm for deciding whether or not a Coxeter element is futuristic? Such an algorithm could conceivably be based on the results of Section 6, which imply that a Coxeter element fails to be futuristic if and only if there is some billiards-plausible closed walk that lifts to a billiards trajectory. Given a billiards-plausible closed walk, one can algorithmically determine whether it lifts to a billiards trajectory. One can also iterate over the billiards-plausible closed walks of a bounded length. So one route to showing that futuristicity is decidable is to find an upper bound for the minimal length of a periodic billiards trajectory or, equivalently, for the minimal length of a billiards-plausible closed walk that lifts.

We remark that there is an algorithm for determining whether or not a given finite convex set $\mathscr{L}$ is heavy with respect to a given Coxeter element $c$ . In order to describe this algorithm, we require a bit of terminology. For $Q\subseteq W$ , let $\mathbf{D}(Q)$ denote the directed labeled graph with vertex set $Q\cup\{\tau_{i}(u):u\in Q,\,i\in I\}$ that has a directed edge labeled $i$ from $u$ to $\tau_{i}(u)$ for all $u\in Q$ and all $i\in I$ . We say that $Q,Q^{\prime}\subseteq W$ are $\tau$ -equivalent if $\mathbf{D}(Q)$ and $\mathbf{D}(Q^{\prime})$ are isomorphic as labeled directed graphs (that is, there exists a graph isomorphism from $\mathbf{D}(Q)$ to $\mathbf{D}(Q^{\prime})$ that preserves the direction and label of each edge).

Let $\mathscr{L}$ be a finite convex set, and let $c$ be a Coxeter element. Recall from Lemma 3.6 that the sizes of the strata are bounded above by $2^{|\Phi\setminus(\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})\cup(-\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})))|}$ . It follows that there are only finitely many distinct proper strata up to $\tau$ -equivalence. It is possible to algorithmically find one representative from each $\tau$ -equivalence class of proper strata. It then suffices to search for periodic billiards trajectories in these representatives. Since each stratum is finite, this search can be completed in a finite amount of time.

### 12.5. Operators from Long Elements

Let $\mathsf{w}_{\circ}$ be a reduced word for the long element of a finite Coxeter group $W$ . Fix a nonempty convex subset $\mathscr{L}$ of $W$ as before. We proved (Theorem 1.22) that $\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}(W)=\mathscr{L}$ . It could be interesting to study the fibers of $\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}$ , even in the special case where $W=\mathfrak{S}_{n}$ and $\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}$ is the extended evacuation operator $\mathrm{Ev}$ .

One could also study the dynamics of the restriction of $\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}$ to $\mathscr{L}$ (which is a bijection). When $W=\mathfrak{S}_{n}$ and $\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}=\mathrm{Ev}$ , the restriction of $\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{0}}$ to $\mathscr{L}$ is Schützenberger’s evacuation map, which is well known to be an involution. In general, however, the restriction of $\tau_{\mathsf{w}_{\circ}}$ to $\mathscr{L}$ need not be an involution.

### 12.6. Sorting Times

Let $c$ be a Coxeter element of $W$ , and let $\mathscr{L}$ be a nonempty finite convex set that is heavy with respect to $c$ . By multiplying $\mathscr{L}$ on the right by an element of $W$ if necessary, we may assume without loss of generality that $\mathbbm{1}\in\mathscr{L}$ . For $u\in W$ , let $\mathrm{T}(u)$ be the smallest nonnegative integer $K$ such that $\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{K}(u)\in\mathscr{L}$ . We call $\mathrm{T}(u)$ the sorting time of $u$ . It is natural to ask about the asymptotic growth rate of $\mathrm{T}(u)$ as $\ell(u)$ grows. (Recall from Section 2 that $\ell(u)$ denotes the length of $u$ .)

Since each noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggle can decrease the length of an element by at most $1$ , it is clear that $\mathrm{T}(u)\geq\ell(u)/|I|-O(1)$ . The finiteness of $\mathscr{L}$ ensures that all strata are finite and that there are only finitely many $\tau$ -equivalence classes of strata (see Section 12.4). Since $\mathscr{L}$ is heavy with respect to $c$ , there exists an integer $k\geq 1$ such that $\mathrm{Sep}(\mathrm{Pro}_{c}^{k}(v))\subsetneq\mathrm{Sep}(v)$ for all $v\in W\setminus\mathscr{L}$ . So, $\mathrm{T}(u)\leq k|\mathrm{Sep}(u)|\leq k\ell(u)$ . This shows that $\mathrm{T}(u)$ grows linearly with $\ell(u)$ .

Even for specific choices of $W$ , $c$ , and $\mathscr{L}$ , it could be interesting to compute or estimate the quantity

$$ C_{0}(c,\mathscr{L}):=\limsup_{\ell(u)\to\infty}\mathrm{T}(u)/\ell(u). $$

Is there an upper bound on $C_{0}(c,\mathscr{L})$ that depends only on $W$ ? One could also study the quantity

$$ \limsup\limits_{\ell(u)\to\infty}\mathrm{T}(u)/|\mathrm{Sep}(u)|, $$

which is closely related to $C_{0}(c,\mathscr{L})$ .

### 12.8. Closed and Antisymmetric Sets of Roots

One can generalize the definition of the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles in Definition 1.2 by replacing the set $\mathrm{R}(\mathscr{L})$ with an arbitrary closed and antisymmetric set $\mathrm{R}\subseteq\Phi$ . Analogues of Lemmas 3.9, 3.10, 5.2 and 5.3 remain true in this more general setting, but Lemmas 3.8 and 3.11 become false.

One special case of this more general setting is that in which $\mathrm{R}=\Phi^{-}$ . In this case, the resulting noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles generate ${\bf H}_{W}(0)$ , the $0$ -Hecke monoid of $W$ , and their action on $W$ defines the standard action of ${\bf H}_{W}(0)$ on $W$ (see [17, 19]). Said differently, $\tau_{\mathsf{w}}(\mathbbm{1})$ is the Demazure product of a word $\mathsf{w}$ .

### 12.9. Other Toggle Sequences

Let $\mathscr{L}$ be a nonempty convex subset of $W$ . Given any infinite sequence ${\bf i}=(i_{1},i_{2},\ldots)$ of elements of $I$ and any starting point $u_{0}\in W$ , we can construct the sequence $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ by the recurrence relation $u_{j}=\tau_{i_{j}}(u_{j-1})$ for all $j\geq 1$ . In this article, we have been primarily concerned with the setting in which ${\bf i}$ arises by repeating some ordering of $I$ . However, it could be fruitful to consider other sequences, such as sequences induced by light beams. We could, for instance, say that ${\bf i}$ is futuristic if for every nonempty finite convex set $\mathscr{L}$ and every starting point $u_{0}$ , the resulting sequence $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},\ldots$ eventually reaches $\mathscr{L}$ . If $\bf i$ is formed by repeating some ordering $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}$ of $I$ , then ${\bf i}$ is futuristic if and only if the Coxeter element $c=s_{i_{n}}\cdots s_{i_{1}}$ is futuristic (by Proposition 1.8).

It could also be interesting to consider the setting in which the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles are applied in a random order. This produces a Markov chain with state space $W$ in which each transition is given by applying $\tau_{i}$ , where $i\in I$ is chosen randomly (according to some probability distribution on $I$ ). This random process was studied by Lam [22] in the case where $W$ is an affine Weyl group and the noninvertible Bender–Knuth toggles are defined via the set $\mathrm{R}=\Phi^{-}$ (as discussed in Section 12.8).
